modules.title: Graduate numerical methods and research practice
modules.prerequisites: Gates B, F and H; rigorous linear algebra, calculus, probability and systems competence.
modules.project: Produce a graduate numerical notebook with derivations, reference implementations, conditioning experiments and a preregistered evaluation plan. Complete substantial assigned problem sets; the short lesson quizzes are only formative checks.

lessons.title: Reading research as claims, assumptions and evidence
lessons.outcome: Extract an implementable argument rather than only a paper summary.
lessons.teach:
A research paper makes claims under assumptions using a method and evidence. First identify the problem, baseline, objective and scope. Then reconstruct the central derivation or algorithm without looking at the authors' code. Track definitions, units and where approximations enter. A result can be valuable while narrower than its abstract initially suggests.
Build a claim-evidence table: each claim points to an equation, proof, experiment or stated limitation. Distinguish reproduction of reported results from an independent implementation and from a new extension. Read related work to identify the actual contribution. Select original papers and author artifacts where available, and record versions. A negative reproduction result needs diagnostic investigation before concluding the original claim is false.
lessons.example: A method reported faster at equal image error is not necessarily faster at equal sample count. Reproducing the wrong comparison target tests a different claim.
lessons.lab: Analyze one paper associated with R23, R44 or R55. Pass: a two-page claim map, a reconstructed central algorithm, at least three assumptions and a feasible reproduction target are reviewed by another reader.
lessons.reading: R23: Further Reading sections for a chosen rendering topic; R44 or R55: one named original paper; handbook research-reading template.

quiz.question: Why distinguish equal-error from equal-sample comparisons?
quiz.answer: They control different quantities and can support different performance conclusions.

quiz.question: What makes a claim-evidence table useful?
quiz.answer: It connects each conclusion to its actual mathematical or experimental support and exposes unsupported generalization.

quiz.question: Does a failed reproduction immediately disprove a paper?
quiz.answer: No. Configuration, implementation, data, numerical and interpretation differences must first be investigated.

sections: Turn a paper into an engineering contract

Write the question as an input-output relationship, not a topic: "For this scene family and error threshold, does method A reach the threshold in less total time than baseline B?" Specify scene motion, resolution, light/material model, numerical precision and the reference used to estimate error. The claim is a predicate over those conditions. An attractive image is an observation; it is not yet the predicate's proof. A reproducible implementation needs enough definitions that a second engineer can construct the same input and decide whether the output passes.

Separate three objects in your notes. The mathematical method defines ideal behavior. The implementation chooses finite precision, data layouts and scheduling. The experiment samples particular workloads on particular machines. A failure in one object does not automatically falsify the other two. For example, an unbiased estimator can be implemented with a wrong density; an accurate implementation can be compared with the wrong quality target. The assigned original papers supply the methods; this contract structure is the course's review procedure. [R44, S05]
Reconstruct before consulting implementation details

On the first pass, collect symbols, domains and units. On the second, derive the central update using a case small enough to calculate by hand. On the third, identify each approximation and each missing engineering choice. Do not hide an omitted detail with a convenient default: record it as an ambiguity and test whether plausible choices change the result. Only then compare your interpretation with author code, supplements or errata.

A claim-evidence map should record the exact figure, equation or artifact supporting each claim; the controlled comparison; one assumption that could break it; and your proposed test. Keep the original claim beside your narrower reproduction claim. This prevents a one-dimensional compliance experiment from becoming a claim to have reproduced a complete cloth benchmark.
Choose a tractable graduate contribution

A useful extension changes one dimension: a new workload distribution, a stricter correctness contract, a memory budget, a failure mode or an algorithmic component. Merely porting code is a contribution to an artifact, but does not by itself demonstrate a new scientific result. Conversely, a rigorous negative result can be valuable when it exposes a boundary and eliminates implementation error as the explanation.

Declare which stage is complete: method reconstruction, result reproduction, extension evaluation or independent review. These labels are deliberately explicit because communities use "reproducibility" and "replicability" differently. Passing the bundled smoke tests establishes none of the later stages on its own. [S14]
expansion.worked: Suppose a baseline has RMSE 0.020 at 4 ms and 0.010 at 16 ms. A candidate has RMSE 0.012 at 4 ms and 0.009 at 8 ms. At the predeclared threshold RMSE <= 0.010, the measured qualifying times are 16 and 8 ms, giving 2x speedup among these tested configurations. At equal 4 ms cost, the candidate has 40% lower RMSE instead. Neither statement establishes its time at exactly 0.010 without another measurement. Record the two claims separately and do not interpolate across a quality curve without stating the interpolation rule.
procedure: Choose XPBD 2016, ReSTIR 2020, or one method explicitly traced through PBRT references. Save the exact author, year, version and retrieval date; link rather than redistribute the paper.
Prepare a two-page claim map with at least three assumptions and one disputed or underspecified implementation choice.
Reconstruct the central algorithm on a scalar or discrete example. Annotate input domains, units, invariants and where approximation enters.
Define one central target, a competent baseline and a failure criterion. Estimate the implementation and evaluation cost before committing.
Ask another reader to identify a claim broader than your evidence. Revise the scope and retain that review comment.
Create an environment record and run the package tests as setup evidence, not as research evidence.
checks: The selected publication and version are unambiguous.
Three assumptions have concrete falsification tests.
The target controls quality, time boundary and workload.
An independent reader reviewed the claim map.
The planned result can be evaluated without inventing unavailable hardware measurements.
problems: P1. An abstract says "4x faster" but the figure measures samples per second, excluding preprocessing. Write a narrower claim and one required end-to-end experiment.
P2. Your reproduction misses the reported value by 15%. Design a diagnostic order that separates estimator, scene, precision, parameter and timing-boundary differences.
solutions: P1. Claim only 4x higher sampling throughput in the reported configuration. Run total preparation plus sample generation plus reconstruction on identical inputs at the same quality threshold; report amortization across reuse counts.

P2. First verify scalar identities and independent-reference agreement. Then match scene/data and parameters, inspect precision and randomization, and audit the timer boundary. Change one factor at a time, retaining both successful and unsuccessful runs. A discrepancy remains unresolved until those controls justify a narrower explanation.
expansion.reading_expanded: R44: abstract, algorithm and evaluation of the 2020 ReSTIR paper; or R55 / S05: XPBD (2016), Sections 3-5. Read the chosen paper in full before finalizing the reproduction boundary. Use S14 for artifact-review vocabulary.

lessons.title: Conditioning, sparse systems and iterative solvers
lessons.outcome: Choose a solver from mathematical properties and error requirements.
lessons.teach:
A linear system Ax=b has numerical behavior governed partly by conditioning: sensitivity of the solution to changes in data. Residual r=b-Ax measures equation mismatch, but a small residual need not imply a small forward error for an ill-conditioned system. Scaling and problem formulation matter before choosing a faster kernel.
Sparse storage exploits structure, while iterative methods use repeated matrix-vector operations. Conjugate gradient requires a symmetric positive-definite setting for its standard guarantees. Preconditioning changes the system seen by the iteration to improve convergence without changing the intended solution when correctly applied. State stopping criteria, norm, precision and maximum work. Test a known solution and increasingly difficult conditioning, not only one friendly matrix.
lessons.example: If A=diag(1,10^-6), its 2-norm condition number is 10^6. A small perturbation in the second equation can produce a much larger relative change in its associated solution component.
lessons.lab: Implement a sparse matrix-vector product and conjugate gradient for a verified SPD system. Pass: derive the relevant assumptions, compare residual and forward error, and evaluate a simple preconditioner over several conditioning levels.
lessons.reading: R54: linear systems, positive definiteness and numerical methods; R07: orthogonality and eigenvalues; R42: numerical optimization background.

quiz.question: What is the 2-norm condition number of diag(1,10^-6)?
Why can a small residual coexist with substantial solution error?
quiz.answer: An ill-conditioned system can amplify small equation perturbations into large changes in the solution.

quiz.question: What matrix property is required by standard conjugate gradient?
quiz.answer: A symmetric positive-definite matrix, or the corresponding Hermitian positive-definite complex case.

sections: Residual, forward error and the condition of the question

Let x* solve Ax*=b and let x be your estimate. Define e=x*-x and r=b-Ax. Then Ae=r, so e=A^-1 r when A is invertible. Using a consistent induced norm, ||e|| <= ||A^-1|| ||r||. Combining ||b|| <= ||A|| ||x*|| yields the relative bound ||e||/||x*|| <= kappa(A) ||r||/||b|| for nonzero b. A residual threshold alone cannot give a useful forward-error guarantee when the condition number is large.

For A=diag(1,10^-6), b=(1,10^-6) and estimate x=(1,0), the residual norm is 10^-6, while the error norm is 1. A small equation mismatch hides a completely wrong second coordinate. The example separates a well-implemented solver from a well-conditioned model. Scaling coordinates, removing redundant constraints and improving boundary conditions may matter more than faster arithmetic.
From a quadratic to preconditioned conjugate gradient

For symmetric positive-definite A, minimize E(x)=0.5 x^T A x-b^T x. Its gradient is Ax-b, and positive curvature gives a unique minimizer. CG constructs search directions that are conjugate under A rather than merely orthogonal in Euclidean space. Standard PCG additionally assumes a fixed SPD preconditioner M. Apply z=M^-1 r; do not explicitly invert a large matrix. A positive diagonal gives the simple Jacobi choice. [S01]

The teaching implementation begins with x=0, r=b, z=M^-1 r and p=z. At each step set alpha=(r^T z)/(p^T A p), update x <- x+alpha p and r <- r-alpha A p, compute z_new=M^-1 r_new, and use beta=(r_new^T z_new)/(r_old^T z_old) to form p_new=z_new+beta p. A nonpositive denominator is a breakdown signal, not a complete SPD test. A nonsymmetric input may slip past that check and still invalidate the derivation.
Storage and stopping are part of the algorithm

Compressed sparse row storage holds row offsets, column indices and nonzero values. Validate offsets, dimensions and index ranges before multiplication. For a tridiagonal problem, sparse multiplication performs work proportional to nonzeros rather than the square of the dimension. The dense solver in this package is an independent oracle for small problems, not a recommended production sparse factorization.

Stop when the measured norm satisfies max(atol,rtol*||b||), or a declared work cap is reached. Recompute the true residual before reporting success because recursive residual updates accumulate error. Report convergence status separately from the solution vector. Your experiments should include a zero right-hand side, a known solution, a poorly scaled SPD family, and an intentionally unsupported matrix. A preconditioner that costs more than it saves in iterations is not automatically an improvement.
expansion.worked: Take A=[[4,1],[1,3]], b=(6,7), x0=0. Then r0=p0=(6,7), A p0=(31,27), r0^T r0=85 and p0^T A p0=375. The first alpha is 85/375=17/75. Thus x1=(1.36,1.5866667), which is not yet the exact solution (1,2). Verify A(1,2)=(6,7). In exact arithmetic CG needs at most two steps here; in floating point the declared tolerance determines whether the measured result is accepted. For the diagonal family in the runner, exact Jacobi scaling makes the preconditioned system the identity, so that special case can converge in one step. It does not establish that Jacobi works well on general sparse systems.
procedure: Derive Ae=r and the relative condition-number bound. Reproduce the diagonal counterexample by hand.
Implement CSR multiplication in the exercise file, checking malformed structures and empty dimensions.
Implement CG/PCG independently and compare a known solution with the dense oracle on small SPD problems.
Sweep condition numbers 1, 100, 10000 and 1000000; compare identity and Jacobi preconditioning.
Log true residual, forward error, iterations, setup time and solve time. Include max-iteration termination.
Add a non-diagonal SPD family to prevent the diagonal preconditioner test from being the whole study.
checks: Known-solution error meets the declared tolerance.
No result is marked converged solely because a loop ended.
Standard CG is not advertised as valid for arbitrary matrices.
Residual and forward error appear separately in raw data.
Preconditioner setup and application costs are retained.
problems: P1. For A=diag(1,10^-6), compute relative residual and relative forward error for b=(1,10^-6), x=(1,0).
P2. Why might a preconditioner that halves iteration count still lose overall time? Give a break-even formula.
solutions: P1. ||r||/||b||=10^-6/sqrt(1+10^-12), approximately 10^-6. ||e||/||x*||=1/sqrt(2), approximately 0.7071. The loose upper bound kappa times relative residual is approximately 1.

P2. Let setup cost be S, original iterations k, original iteration cost c and extra preconditioner application cost m. It wins only if S+(k/2)(c+m)<kc. For one solve, expensive setup can dominate; for repeated right-hand sides, state how setup is amortized.
expansion.reading_expanded: R54: positive-definite equilibrium systems; S01: Shewchuk, Sections 3, 8, 11-12 and Appendix B3; R42: numerical linear algebra background. Re-derive the two-dimensional update without copying implementation code.

lessons.title: Constrained optimization, derivatives and optimality conditions
lessons.outcome: Derive and verify an optimization method for an engineering objective.
lessons.teach:
Optimization requires a defined objective, feasible set and numerical tolerance. For differentiable unconstrained problems, stationary points have zero gradient but may be minima, maxima or saddles. Convexity provides stronger global conclusions under the appropriate assumptions. Equality and inequality constraints introduce Lagrange multipliers and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, whose necessity or sufficiency depends on regularity and convexity.
For nonlinear least squares, residual Jacobians support Gauss-Newton-style approximations; poor scaling or rank deficiency can require damping or regularization. Check analytic or automatic derivatives against finite differences over sensible step sizes. Gradient checks themselves have truncation and roundoff error. Report convergence histories and failed initializations rather than only a final successful parameter set.
lessons.example: Minimize x^2+y^2 subject to x+y=1. The Lagrangian gives 2x+lambda=0 and 2y+lambda=0; together with the constraint, x=y=0.5 and lambda=-1.
lessons.lab: Derive the example, then solve a constrained fitting or IK problem with a numerical method. Pass: derivative checks, feasibility residual, convergence criteria and at least one failure or sensitivity case are reported.
lessons.reading: R42: convexity, duality, optimality and numerical methods; R41: gradients and constrained differentials.

quiz.question: What is the constrained minimizer in the example?
quiz.answer: x=y=0.5, with objective 0.5 and multiplier -1 under the stated Lagrangian sign convention.

quiz.question: Does zero gradient prove a general nonconvex point is a minimum?
quiz.answer: No. It may also be a saddle or maximum.

quiz.question: Why vary finite-difference step size in a derivative check?
quiz.answer: Large steps incur truncation error while extremely small steps amplify floating-point roundoff.

sections: State the optimization problem before choosing an optimizer

A fitting problem needs an objective, a feasible set and a parameterization. A low loss can coexist with impossible joint angles, a negative material coefficient or an invalid energy model. For f(x) with inequalities g_i(x)<=0 and equalities h_j(x)=0, write L=f+sum(lambda_i g_i)+sum(nu_j h_j). KKT combines primal feasibility, lambda_i>=0, stationarity of L and lambda_i g_i=0. Necessity needs appropriate regularity conditions; in convex problems, a feasible KKT point provides a global optimum under the standard convex formulation. Do not promote every stationary point to a minimum. [S02]

For an equality constraint, the multiplier is not constrained to be positive. Its sign depends on the chosen equality convention. Changing x+y-1 to 1-x-y reverses the multiplier sign without changing the solution. Numerical checks should compare stationarity and feasibility, not only a memorized multiplier.
Derive a solver you can independently verify

Minimize 0.5||x-t||^2 subject to sum(x)=s. Stationarity gives x_i-t_i+lambda=0. Summing yields lambda=(sum(t)-s)/n, so x=t-lambda*1. This affine projection is the executable reference; it is not a general nonlinear constrained solver. With t=(0.2,0.9), s=1, lambda=0.05 and x=(0.15,0.85).

For nonlinear least squares 0.5||r(theta)||^2, the gradient is J^T r and the exact Hessian is J^T J+sum(r_i Hessian(r_i)). Gauss-Newton neglects the second term; damping solves a modified system such as (J^T J+mu I)delta=-J^T r. Poorly scaled parameters, rank deficiency and large residuals can make a naive step ineffective. A line search or trust region evaluates whether the step actually improves the intended objective.
Differentiate a game-relevant model, not just a toy polynomial

For a planar two-link arm, p(theta)=(l1 cos(t1)+l2 cos(t1+t2), l1 sin(t1)+l2 sin(t1+t2)). Its first Jacobian column differentiates both links, while the second differentiates only the second link. A straight arm can lose local ability to move in one Cartesian direction: the Jacobian becomes poorly conditioned. This links inverse kinematics to Lesson 41.2 instead of treating optimizer failure as magic.

Check each derivative using centered differences at several step sizes, preferably away from discontinuities. A tolerance should reflect scale: compare absolute error near zero and relative error when the derivative is substantial. Then deliberately test a singular pose, an unreachable target and a bound-active solution. Preserve the failure report. An optimizer that returns a status and feasible fallback is more useful than one that silently returns its last iterate.
expansion.worked: For the manifest problem f=x^2+y^2, h=x+y-1, stationarity is 2x+lambda=0 and 2y+lambda=0. Subtracting gives x=y; feasibility gives x=y=0.5 and lambda=-1. The objective is 0.5. Along the feasible line y=1-x, f=2(x-0.5)^2+0.5, which independently proves the unique minimizer. For a centered derivative check of x^3 at x=2, [(2+h)^3-(2-h)^3]/(2h)=12+h^2 in exact arithmetic. This shows the truncation term explicitly; floating-point cancellation adds a different error as h becomes very small.
procedure: Derive the equality-constrained example and implement the affine projection without a generic optimizer.
Write gradient checks for a quadratic, the two-link arm residual and a selected fitting objective.
Implement a damped least-squares or projected constrained fitting/IK experiment beyond the supplied affine oracle.
Record feasibility, stationarity or projected-gradient residual, objective history and termination reason.
Sweep initialization, finite-difference step size and one scale parameter.
Add an unreachable or rank-deficient case and design an explicit fallback rather than mislabeling it convergence.
checks: The Lagrangian sign convention is recorded.
Both objective quality and constraint feasibility are tested.
Derivative checks cover a range of step sizes.
A nonconvex stationary point is not assumed globally optimal.
The full lab extends beyond the provided closed-form projection.
problems: P1. Project t=(1,2,4) onto sum(x)=1. Is the result also a projection onto the probability simplex?
P2. Derive the two columns of the two-link arm Jacobian and identify a singular pose for unit links.
solutions: P1. lambda=(7-1)/3=2; x=(-1,0,2). It satisfies the affine constraint but is not in the probability simplex because one component is negative. Nonnegativity requires an additional constrained projection.

P2. Column one is (-l1 sin(t1)-l2 sin(t1+t2), l1 cos(t1)+l2 cos(t1+t2)); column two is (-l2 sin(t1+t2),l2 cos(t1+t2)). At t2=0 the columns are parallel, so rank is at most one and the local inverse is singular.

lessons.title: Experimental design, uncertainty and reproducible graduate work
lessons.outcome: Make a performance or quality claim that survives independent scrutiny.
lessons.teach:
Define the primary outcome and comparison before examining final results. Choose workloads that represent the intended claim, plus adverse and held-out cases. Repeated frames within one run can be correlated, so the statistical unit might be a run, scene or device rather than every frame. A large count of correlated observations does not automatically provide strong independent evidence.
Use confidence intervals or other justified uncertainty summaries, report effect sizes and preserve raw observations. Ablations remove or replace components to test which parts cause an improvement. Multiple comparisons and parameter tuning can overfit the benchmark suite. Keep final evaluation data separate from tuning when feasible. State external validity limits, including devices, workloads and quality settings not tested.
lessons.example: Ten thousand frames from one scene are not equivalent to ten thousand independent games. A scene-level comparison across diverse scenes can better test a claim about broad engine behavior.
lessons.lab: Preregister a small experiment with baseline, primary metric, trial unit and exclusion policy. Pass: raw data and analysis scripts reproduce the tables, and an ablation isolates at least one proposed mechanism.
lessons.reading: R09: statistical inference; R42: experimental examples; handbook benchmark and research templates.

quiz.question: Why identify the statistical unit?
quiz.answer: It determines what observations can reasonably be treated as independent for the intended inference.

quiz.question: What does an ablation test?
quiz.answer: Whether removing or changing a component changes the outcome in a way that supports its claimed contribution.

quiz.question: Why reserve held-out workloads?
quiz.answer: They test whether tuning improvements generalize beyond the cases used to choose parameters.

sections: Define what an observation represents

The unit of inference is the object your claim generalizes over. Frames nested in one run share scene content, thermal history and scheduling behavior. Treating every frame as an independent experiment artificially increases apparent evidence. A study about scenes may need a scene-level summary; a study about repeated execution on one machine may use independent process runs. State the hierarchy explicitly: device, scene, run and frame. [R09]

Pair a baseline and candidate on the same workload when this removes irrelevant variation. Randomize execution order to reduce systematic warmup or drift effects. Keep the seed policy fixed and explain common-random-number pairing when it is used. A run killed by an unrelated system failure may be excluded under a predefined rule; a slow run caused by the method itself is a result, not an inconvenience.
Effect size, uncertainty and diagnostic evidence

For positive paired times a_i and b_i, log speedups z_i=log(a_i/b_i) have a useful additive scale. Report exp(mean(z_i)) when a geometric-mean speedup is the chosen estimand. It is not the same as sum(a_i)/sum(b_i), which answers a total-time question. The included bootstrap resamples whole pairs and returns percentile bounds. Its numerical output cannot establish independence, repair a biased workload suite or justify a sample size.

The bundled native benchmark is a within-process diagnostic, with 12 randomized-order pairs. Those rows demonstrate data capture and timer boundaries; they are not enough to claim broad CPU or GPU superiority. For an actual study, repeat independent processes, retain environment records and justify how uncertainty is calculated at the intended unit. State the confidence procedure rather than treating a 95% interval as a 95% probability statement about a fixed unknown parameter.
Ablations and sensitivity answer different questions

An ablation removes or replaces a component while preserving other controls. A sensitivity sweep changes a parameter to reveal the boundary of an effect. Both can be misleading when quality changes simultaneously with time. Compare a denoiser with and without history at equal total budget, and also disclose the resulting error; do not call a quality loss a pure optimization.

Reserve final scenes or workload families before tuning. Choose the main metric, analysis, exclusions and stopping rule before examining the final comparison. Keep secondary findings labeled exploratory. Publish raw rows, not only a plotted mean, and give the reviewer a command that regenerates the table from those rows. Failure to reproduce a timing exactly is not automatically a failure to reproduce the engineering conclusion; define acceptable numerical and statistical agreement in advance.
expansion.worked: Two paired workloads take baseline times (10,100) ms and candidate times (5,90) ms. The geometric-mean speedup is sqrt(2*(100/90)), approximately 1.491x. The total-time speedup is 110/95, approximately 1.158x. Both calculations are correct but weight the workloads differently. A presentation that switches between them after seeing the data changes the question. If each value was itself the mean of 1000 correlated frames, those 4000 frames do not automatically provide 4000 independent speedup observations.
procedure: Fill PREREGISTRATION.md before collecting new performance results. Name the primary metric, target population, trial unit, paired design and exclusion policy.
Collect a small pilot to estimate noise and runtime; use it to set a feasible sample plan without treating it as the final test.
Keep final workloads separate from parameter selection. Execute baseline and candidate in randomized order.
Retain raw observations and calculate the chosen effect size with an uncertainty method suitable for the unit.
Run one ablation and one parameter sensitivity sweep; report failures and missing cells.
Give a reviewer the raw CSV and analysis command; ask them to regenerate the main table without editing values.
checks: The independent unit is justified rather than inferred from row count.
The main metric and timer boundaries were declared before the final comparison.
All exclusions and failed configurations are listed.
Ablation and sensitivity are distinct.
A reviewer can regenerate the analysis from raw data.
problems: P1. One scene produces 10000 frames and another produces 100. How could a frame-weighted mean distort a claim about typical scenes?
P2. Why is the fixed-ratio bootstrap unit test not evidence that the experimental method is statistically sound?
solutions: P1. The first scene receives 100 times the weight, even if the intended population treats scenes equally. Summarize within scene and use a justified scene-level aggregation, or explicitly define the workload-weighted estimand.

P2. The unit test checks arithmetic and reproducibility for known inputs. It does not test independence, representative sampling, exclusion rules, tuning leakage, interval coverage under the actual design or the adequacy of the sample size.
expansion.reading_expanded: R09: inference, confidence intervals and experimental units; S14: artifact evaluation. Use the package PREREGISTRATION and BENCHMARK_MANIFEST templates before collecting final data.

modules.title: Advanced parallel and GPU algorithms
modules.project: Implement a reusable GPU reduction, scan or compaction primitive and integrate it into an engine workload. Compare a simple reference, a competent library baseline when available and your implementation at equal correctness requirements.

lessons.title: Parallel reductions, scans and work-span analysis
lessons.outcome: Prove the structure of a parallel primitive before tuning it.
lessons.teach:
A reduction combines many values with an operator; a scan produces prefix combinations. Associativity supports regrouping mathematically, but floating-point addition is not exactly associative. Decide whether the contract requires bitwise reproducibility, bounded error or an exact integer result. A tree reduction can reduce dependency depth from linear to logarithmic while retaining linear total work.
Work is the total number of operations; span is the longest dependency chain. More processors cannot beat the span without changing the algorithm. A naive parallel scan can have extra logarithmic work, while work-efficient constructions achieve linear work with logarithmic span under their model. Handle partial groups, empty inputs and irregular sizes explicitly. Cross-group coordination must follow the API rather than assuming a global barrier inside an ordinary dispatch.
lessons.example: A balanced reduction over 1,024 elements has 10 combination levels under a binary-tree model and 1,023 total pairwise combinations. Its implementation still pays memory and synchronization costs.
lessons.lab: Implement reduction and either scan or compaction. Pass: derive work/span bounds, test sizes 0, 1 and non-powers of two, and report the numerical/reproducibility contract.
lessons.reading: R37: cooperative execution and synchronization; R48: parallel architectures; derive algorithm bounds using Module 14 methods.

quiz.question: How many levels are in a balanced binary reduction of 1,024 values?
How many pairwise combines does that reduction require?
Why can parallel floating-point sums differ from serial sums?
quiz.answer: Changing grouping changes rounding because floating-point addition is not exactly associative.

sections: Work, span and the algebraic contract

Represent the computation as a directed acyclic graph. Work W counts all operations; span S is the longest dependency path. On P ideal processors the runtime cannot be below max(W/P,S). This is a lower bound in a declared model, not a hardware prediction: memory bandwidth, launch overhead, occupancy and barriers add constraints.

A reduction needs an identity and an associative operator for arbitrary regrouping. Integer addition modulo 2^32 is associative; real addition is associative; finite-precision floating-point addition is not exactly associative. Choose the numerical contract before changing order. Determinism on one fixed tree is weaker than agreement with every serial sum or every device. The Python scan uses arbitrary-precision integers, whereas the native and CUDA examples use uint32 wraparound. Their domains agree only when you account for that difference.
Derive exclusive scan through two tree passes

For inputs (3,1,7,0,4), an exclusive sum scan is (0,3,4,11,11). The value at position i is the reduction over positions strictly before i. In an upsweep, each tree node stores the sum of its children. Set the root to the identity, then walk downward: the left child receives the parent's prefix; the right child receives the parent's prefix plus the saved left-subtree sum. This preserves the left-to-right order even for associative operators that are not commutative. [S03]

Padding a non-power-of-two input with identities simplifies a teaching implementation. If the padded size is m, the two passes use 2(m-1) combines and logarithmic depth. Since n<=m<2n for n>0, work remains O(n). Do not apply log2(0); the empty scan returns an empty sequence. The exercise should establish those cases before adding dispatch-level hierarchy.
From scan to engine compaction

A stable compaction converts visibility flags to destination offsets using exclusive scan. Write each kept element once at its offset. The output count is the last offset plus the last flag for a nonempty input. Stability matters when later processing assumes original draw order or deterministic entity ordering.

A GPU hierarchy scans chunks, scans their totals in another dispatch and adds each chunk's offset. A normal thread-block barrier does not synchronize arbitrary blocks. Do not implement a global spin barrier that assumes all blocks can be resident. The optional CUDA reference instead performs multi-dispatch reduction, with out-of-range lanes supplying zero and every lane reaching each block barrier. It is supplied for hardware validation and was not compiled in this environment. [S04]
expansion.worked: For n=1024, a complete binary reduction performs 1023 additions with 10 combine levels. An exclusive scan built from upsweep and downsweep on 1024 leaves uses 2046 additions in this simple model. With n=1025 padded to m=2048, it uses 4094 additions, still linear in n but almost twice the previous work for one extra input. That discontinuity is a reason to benchmark boundary sizes rather than only powers of two. For flags (1,0,1,1), offsets are (0,1,1,2); kept entries go to output slots 0,1,2.
procedure: State identity, associativity and overflow/rounding behavior for the selected operator. Derive work/span bounds.
Implement reduction and exclusive scan or stable compaction without using the reference implementation as your submitted work.
Test sizes 0,1,3,31,32,33,1023,1024,1025 and a large irregular size. Include all-false and all-true flags.
Compare with the serial oracle under the declared numerical contract. Add a floating-point experiment that intentionally demonstrates order dependence.
For the GPU route, use multiple dispatches for global hierarchy and validate every boundary lane. Run device error and memory checks where supported.
Integrate the primitive into a visibility, active-particle or entity-filtering workload; retain setup and result-consumption costs.
checks: Empty and partial groups behave correctly.
The proof covers non-power-of-two sizes.
No ordinary dispatch relies on an unsupported global barrier.
Integer versus floating-point contracts are explicit.
GPU completion is marked pending until device execution is actually verified.
problems: P1. Derive the output length of compaction from flags and exclusive offsets without a second full sum.
P2. Give floating-point values for which regrouping changes the result, then explain why this does not invalidate an exact-integer scan test.
solutions: P1. For n>0, length=offset[n-1]+flag[n-1]. For n=0 it is zero. Each kept position has a distinct count of earlier kept positions, proving unique writes and stability.

P2. Under a typical floating format, (10^20+(-10^20))+3 can yield 3 while 10^20+((-10^20)+3) can yield 0. The rounded algebra differs from exact integers or modulo arithmetic. A correct test must use the contract of the implementation being tested.

lessons.title: Tiling, data reuse and asynchronous pipelines
lessons.outcome: Overlap movement and computation without creating races.
lessons.teach:
Tiling partitions a computation so values can be reused in a faster memory level. Matrix multiplication, image filters and neighborhood operations benefit when the tile fits available storage and exposes sufficient parallelism. Larger tiles can increase reuse but also raise register or shared-memory demand and reduce residency.
Double buffering can overlap preparation of one tile with computation on another. The pipeline needs explicit ownership: no consumer reads an incomplete tile and no producer overwrites data still in use. Asynchronous copy features vary by device; maintain a correct portable baseline. Account for boundary tiles, alignment, synchronization and extra staging work. Compare arithmetic intensity at the memory level actually being optimized.
lessons.example: For C=A*B, reusing a loaded A or B tile across many multiply-adds can raise useful operations per byte. A tile that spills heavily can erase that advantage.
lessons.lab: Implement a tiled matrix multiply or image filter, then one overlap variant where supported. Pass: adversarial dimensions match the reference, synchronization is checked and the end-to-end comparison includes staging overhead.
lessons.reading: R37: shared memory, synchronization and asynchronous operations where supported; R43: operational intensity.

quiz.question: Why can larger tiles hurt performance?
quiz.answer: They can increase resource usage, reduce residency or cause spills and boundary overhead.

quiz.question: What ownership rule is essential for double buffering?
quiz.answer: A buffer must not be consumed before preparation completes or overwritten before its current consumer finishes.

quiz.question: Why retain a non-asynchronous baseline?
quiz.answer: It provides a simpler correctness and portability reference for evaluating the extra pipeline complexity.

sections: Count reuse at the memory boundary you intend to optimize

A square B-by-B matrix-multiplication tile performs about 2B^3 arithmetic operations while loading two B-by-B input tiles for one inner-product stage. With 4-byte elements, that idealized stage moves 8B^2 input bytes, giving B/4 operations per input byte. This count deliberately excludes output traffic, boundary waste, staging and repeated loads at other memory levels. Never compare that optimistic intensity with a complete measured kernel as though the boundaries were identical.

For B=32, the two input tiles need 8192 bytes; double buffering them needs 16384 bytes before padding or additional metadata. Larger B increases reuse in the model but consumes more shared storage and registers. A tile that reduces active resident work or spills registers can lose even when the operation-to-input-byte ratio improves. Use measured bottlenecks to explain a result rather than merely saying "shared memory is faster." [R43, S04]
A pipeline is an ownership protocol

Name buffer states: free, filling, ready and consuming. The producer may reuse a slot only after the previous consumer finishes. The consumer may begin only after the copy's completion event, not merely after issue. Double buffering alternates slots, but alternating indices alone does not establish either dependency.

The reference schedule has one copy engine, one compute engine and two slots. For tile i, copy begins after both the copy engine and that slot are free. Compute begins after the tile is ready and the compute engine is free. This creates an executable timing/ownership model, not actual asynchronous hardware execution. A device implementation must translate every model edge into the API's synchronization contract and handle the first and last stage explicitly.
Prove correctness before measuring overlap

Boundary tiles need predicates for each load and store. Every thread participating in a block barrier must follow a compatible control path. Zero-fill out-of-range contributions rather than letting a few lanes return before a collective barrier. Include rectangular matrices such as 5x3 multiplied by 3x7 so that every dimension has a partial tile.

For a performance comparison, separate allocation, host preparation, transfer, kernel execution and result consumption. Then measure the end-to-end path directly: overlapping stage times cannot simply be summed. A faster steady-state pipeline can still lose for one tile because fill/drain overhead dominates. Keep a non-overlapped implementation for correctness and unsupported hardware, and log why capability dispatch selected each path. [S04]
expansion.worked: Assume a copy takes 2 time units and computation takes 5 per tile, with independent engines and two available slots. Eight serial tiles take 8*(2+5)=56 units. The ideal pipeline takes 2+8*5=42 units: copy tile 0, then let later copies overlap computation. The model speedup is 56/42=1.333x. This is a prediction under stated assumptions, not a measured GPU result. If staging adds 2 units to each compute stage, the same model becomes 2+8*7=58 units and loses to the original serial schedule.
procedure: Derive tile storage and intensity for at least three tile sizes, labeling included and omitted traffic.
Implement a tiled multiply or filter and verify against a straightforward reference on rectangular and ragged dimensions.
Run pipeline_trace and check that no slot is overwritten before its prior consumer ends. Draw or tabulate the dependency sequence.
Implement one overlap variant only on a supported API/device; otherwise submit the model and mark the device experiment pending.
Measure one-tile, many-tile and boundary-heavy regimes with staging included.
Investigate a losing tile size; explain the loss with resource usage or an explicitly testable hypothesis.
checks: The numerical output matches the declared tolerance.
Every buffer has an explicit producer-to-consumer and consumer-to-reuse edge.
Boundary work does not bypass required barriers.
Modeled timings are labeled separately from measurements.
The fallback path remains tested.
problems: P1. Under the stated 4-byte ideal stage model, compute intensity and double-buffer storage for B=16 and B=64.
P2. Four tiles take copy=6 and compute=2 units. Derive ideal serial and two-buffer pipelined completion times.
solutions: P1. B=16 gives 4 operations/input-byte and 16B^2=4096 bytes of double-buffered input storage. B=64 gives 16 operations/input-byte and 65536 bytes. These are model counts, not feasibility or occupancy guarantees.
P2. Serial time is 4*(6+2)=32. Copy is the bottleneck, so the ideal pipeline is 4*6+2=26, including the final compute drain. Required ownership and engine independence must hold.

lessons.title: Irregular workloads, wavefront scheduling and load balance
lessons.outcome: Design around variable work rather than assuming identical threads.
lessons.teach:
Ray traversal, graph processing and variable-length simulation tasks have irregular work. A fixed assignment can leave some workers idle while a few long tasks dominate the tail. Work queues, compaction and wavefront processing reorganize active tasks, trading scheduling and memory traffic for better coherence or load balance.
Persistent-worker designs keep workers alive to fetch tasks, but need bounded queues, termination detection and a memory-ordering contract. Global progress cannot depend on every workgroup being resident when the hardware does not guarantee that. Sorting tasks by similarity can improve coherence but has a cost and can alter latency. Evaluate both balanced and skewed distributions, including rare expensive tasks.
lessons.example: If 99 tasks take 1 unit and one takes 100 units, static one-task assignments can leave the final completion dominated by the long task. Splitting or scheduling work differently may help only when the task is divisible.
lessons.lab: Implement an irregular workload using static assignment and a queue or compaction alternative. Pass: prove or test termination, handle queue capacity safely and measure tail behavior as well as mean throughput.
lessons.reading: R37: execution, atomics and synchronization; R48: multithreaded scheduling; R23: wavefront rendering as an application.

quiz.question: Why can average task cost hide poor completion time?
quiz.answer: A few long tasks can dominate the final tail after most workers become idle.

quiz.question: Why avoid a global spin barrier requiring every group to be resident?
quiz.answer: Unschedulable groups may never run while resident groups wait, causing deadlock.

quiz.question: Is sorting tasks always beneficial?
quiz.answer: No. Sorting cost, added latency and data movement can exceed coherence gains.

sections: Throughput can look healthy while the last job dominates

For indivisible jobs with costs c_i on P workers, completion time is at least max(sum(c_i)/P,max(c_i)). A queue can redistribute jobs, but cannot make an indivisible 100-unit job finish in 10 units. Start by identifying whether a long task can be split: a ray path can move through bounded stages; a blocking external operation may not be divisible by your scheduler.

Static assignment minimizes scheduling overhead and can preserve locality. Dynamic assignment fills idle workers but adds atomic traffic, metadata movement and termination complexity. Distribution matters: uniform costs, a heavy tail and a spatially clustered hotspot can favor different strategies even at the same mean. Report makespan, queue depth and late-job latency in addition to operations per second.
Wavefront processing changes the unit of work

A monolithic path-tracing kernel carries different rays through intersection, material evaluation and secondary-ray generation. A wavefront approach places active work in stage-specific queues. This can improve coherence at a stage while increasing intermediate state traffic and dispatch cost. Compaction from Lesson 42.1 removes inactive entries between stages. Sorting by material or region adds yet another tradeoff. [S06]

For each queue, state capacity, producer count, consumer count and payload lifetime. Reserving a slot and publishing an initialized payload are different events. A consumer must not read the payload merely because an index was incremented if publication has not established the required ordering. A bounded queue must return a safe overflow/backpressure outcome, not silently overwrite live entries.
Termination needs more than an empty snapshot

An empty work queue does not prove the computation is finished while a worker can still publish descendants. One design tracks queued plus in-flight work under an ordering protocol; completion requires both to be zero with no new source admitted. Another bounds work by explicit dispatch stages and terminates when the next active count is zero. The correct choice depends on whether jobs create jobs and what progress the API guarantees.

Persistent GPU workers are not a license to spin on global barriers. Resident groups can occupy resources while waiting for groups that cannot start. Use an API-supported cooperative execution contract, a staged launch or a proof that does not require simultaneous residency. The included scheduling function models cost allocation only; it does not validate a concurrent queue, GPU memory ordering or global progress. Those remain implementation obligations. [S04]
expansion.worked: For costs (100,1,1,...,1) with 99 one-unit jobs and 8 workers, total work is 199. The average-work lower bound is 24.875, but the indivisible-job bound is 100, so no scheduler in this model can finish below 100. Round-robin static assignment gives the first worker 100 plus 12 short jobs, for 112. A queue that starts the long job immediately can finish the rest before it, approaching 100 without dispatch overhead. Moving the long job late in queue order or charging queue costs changes the result. This is a workload model, not a measured GPU speedup.
procedure: Define the job unit and whether jobs are divisible or can spawn more jobs. Derive lower bounds.
Compare static assignment and queue/compaction alternatives on uniform, skewed and burst-arrival distributions.
Add a queue-capacity contract and a documented termination protocol to your actual implementation.
Create a trace that separates waiting time, service time and final completion.
Stress all-idle, full-queue, one-giant-job and jobs-spawning-jobs cases where applicable.
Measure scheduling and sorting overhead; integrate into an engine workload rather than timing only an empty queue.
checks: Every accepted job is completed or explicitly canceled, never lost or duplicated.
Queue capacity cannot be exceeded silently.
Termination accounts for in-flight producers.
The analysis states the indivisible-work lower bound.
No model-only timing is presented as a device result.
problems: P1. Show why an empty queue while one job is executing is insufficient evidence of termination.
P2. A reordering stage costs 0.8 ms and saves 0.5 ms of traversal. When could it still be justified, and what would need measurement?
solutions: P1. The executing job can later publish another job. Terminating at the empty snapshot discards valid work. A correct protocol must include in-flight work and establish that no future producer remains.

P2. It loses 0.3 ms under the stated one-frame timing boundary. It could be justified by another measured benefit, such as lower tail latency or reuse across multiple queries, but that changes the claim and requires a complete accounting of costs and quality.

lessons.title: Portable performance and integration-quality evaluation
lessons.outcome: Separate algorithmic benefit from one device-specific tuning win.
lessons.teach:
A performance-portable implementation preserves correctness and obtains useful efficiency across its stated target set. This does not mean identical code or identical speed everywhere. Capability dispatch can select specialized paths while keeping a tested fallback. Tuning parameters should be bounded and recorded rather than silently selected from the final test set.
Compare against a competent baseline and include small, large and irregular workloads. Report speed, memory, numerical error and integration cost. A kernel that is faster only after excluding transfer or conversion work should make that boundary explicit. Reproducible artifacts include build scripts, device capability reports, raw data and failure cases. Lack of access to multiple GPUs is a limitation to disclose, not a reason to invent portability evidence.
lessons.example: A tile size tuned on one GPU can reduce occupancy or exceed shared-memory limits on another. Capability checks and independent tuning prevent that choice from becoming an invalid universal default.
lessons.lab: Integrate the selected primitive into the engine and evaluate at least two workload regimes. Pass: application impact is measured, unsupported features fall back safely and any untested device claims are explicitly excluded.
lessons.reading: R37 and R21: capability contracts; R43: performance models; Module 41 experimental protocol.

quiz.question: Does portable performance require one fixed launch configuration?
quiz.answer: No. Valid specialization or bounded tuning may be necessary across targets.

quiz.question: What should be said when only one GPU was tested?
quiz.answer: The evidence is limited to that tested configuration; broader portability remains unverified.

quiz.question: Why measure integration cost?
quiz.answer: A standalone kernel gain may not survive real data preparation, scheduling and result consumption.

sections: Portability has at least three separate questions

Functional portability asks whether the implementation is valid on the supported target set. Performance portability asks whether it retains useful efficiency across that set. Artifact portability asks whether another engineer can build and run it. One source file that compiles on two devices answers none of these questions completely.

Describe the target set explicitly: API, feature level, precision, storage limits and subgroup assumptions. Specialize only behind capability checks. A tile fitting on device A may be invalid on B, even before performance is considered. Avoid using a single vendor's execution width as a language-level invariant. Keep a baseline that satisfies the same numerical contract and report the reason for every fallback. [S04, R21]
The application upper bound comes before heroic kernel work

Suppose a primitive accounts for fraction f of total baseline time and is accelerated by s, with all other work unchanged. The ideal application speedup is 1/((1-f)+f/s). This derives directly from adding the unchanged and accelerated fractions; it excludes integration overhead. For f=0.2 and s=4, the maximum under those assumptions is 1/0.85, approximately 1.176x. Any added data conversion reduces that benefit.

Roofline provides a different bound: attainable arithmetic rate is no more than min(peak arithmetic rate, measured bandwidth times arithmetic intensity) under its model. Combine the two views rather than using either as a proof of achieved speed. A kernel can be bandwidth-limited while also being unimportant to the frame's critical path. [R43]
A fair comparison is a maintained artifact

Use a competent library baseline when available and disclose its version and configuration. Separate allocation, transfers, conversion, synchronization and computation; then time the end-to-end operation as used by the engine. Report small workloads where launch overhead dominates, large workloads where bandwidth matters, and irregular workloads that expose boundaries.

An untested device is a blank evidence cell, not a predicted pass. When only one GPU is available, evaluate multiple workloads on that device and narrow the claim. A CPU model can verify indexing or algebra, but cannot certify GPU performance portability. The package's native benchmark deliberately compares two CPU algorithms and preserves losses; it is a training artifact for measuring honestly, not a sales claim about a universal winner.
expansion.worked: A frame takes 10 ms: 2 ms is the selected primitive and 8 ms is other work. A 4x primitive produces 8+0.5=8.5 ms, giving 1.176x application speedup. Now add 0.7 ms of packing and 0.4 ms of synchronization: the frame is 9.6 ms, only 1.042x faster. A report showing only the 2-to-0.5 ms kernel chart hides almost all of the engineering conclusion. If a different scene spends just 0.2 ms in the original primitive, the same fixed integration cost can turn the candidate into a regression.
procedure: Define a capability matrix with tested, unsupported and untested states. Never collapse them into one pass/fail column.
Integrate the chosen primitive into a minimal engine workload with a fallback path.
Record compiler, library, driver, device and launch configuration locally; do not borrow another machine's limits.
Benchmark small, large and irregular regimes against a competent baseline at the same numerical contract.
Compare predicted application benefit with measured total latency and memory footprint.
Write a one-page decision that includes a losing case, scope limitations and the maintenance cost of specialization.
checks: The fallback passes the same functional tests.
Performance claims name the tested target set.
The chosen baseline is not intentionally weakened.
Kernel and end-to-end boundaries are both visible.
No unavailable GPU result is filled with a CPU timing.
problems: P1. If f=0.05, what is the largest possible application speedup even with an infinitely fast kernel and no overhead?
P2. Distinguish unsupported from untested in a device capability matrix and explain why that distinction matters.
solutions: P1. The limit is 1/(1-0.05)=1.05263x. Eliminating only 5% of runtime cannot justify a claimed 2x application improvement under the same workload.

P2. Unsupported means a known required capability is absent or deliberately excluded; untested means evidence has not been collected. The latter cannot justify either a success claim or a categorical assertion of incompatibility.

modules.title: Advanced rendering and reconstruction
modules.project: Reproduce a bounded rendering result and add one justified extension. Derive the estimator or reconstruction objective, compare equal-quality cost, include temporal failure cases and preserve source scenes and evaluation scripts.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo light transport and multiple importance sampling
lessons.outcome: Derive estimators with correct densities and measures.
lessons.teach:
The rendering equation expresses outgoing radiance as emission plus an integral of incident radiance, scattering and geometry factors. Monte Carlo estimation samples an integral: for samples from density p, average f(x)/p(x) where p is positive over the relevant nonzero support. Correct units and probability measures matter; area and solid-angle densities are not interchangeable without a Jacobian.
Importance sampling aims to reduce variance by matching useful structure. Multiple importance sampling combines strategies with weights that sum appropriately under the estimator. The balance heuristic uses relative weighted densities, but sample counts and support must be included correctly. Russian roulette can terminate paths without bias when surviving contributions receive the proper probability compensation. Finite-variance independent sampling gives the familiar inverse-square-root standard-error scaling; do not assume it for every estimator.
lessons.example: With one sample from each of two strategies and densities p1=2 and p2=6 at a point, the balance weight for strategy 1 is 2/(2+6)=0.25.
lessons.lab: Implement a path tracer with explicit light sampling and MIS. Pass: derive the estimator, verify a simple known integral, compare variance at equal cost and test emission and grazing-angle edge cases.
lessons.reading: R23: Monte Carlo Integration, Light Transport and sampling strategies. Work the associated mathematical exercises, not only the implementation.

quiz.question: What is the balance weight for strategy 1 in the example?
quiz.answer: 0.25 under equal sample counts.

quiz.question: Why is p(x)>0 on relevant support important?
quiz.answer: Otherwise nonzero contributions can never be sampled and the estimator can be biased or undefined.

quiz.question: What sample-count increase ideally halves standard error for independent finite-variance samples?
quiz.answer: Approximately four times as many samples.

sections: An estimator is a mathematical object, not a bag of samples

For I=integral f(x) dx and samples X drawn from density p with respect to that same measure, E[f(X)/p(X)]=I when support and integrability conditions hold. A density is not a probability at a point; its units depend on the domain. In light transport, scattering terms, cosine factors, emitted radiance and visibility combine into an integrand. Losing one factor can produce plausible images while estimating the wrong quantity.

For a sampled light surface point, solid angle and surface area satisfy d_omega=abs(cos_light)/distance^2 * d_area. Therefore p_omega=p_area*distance^2/abs(cos_light). Light-selection probability is another factor: choosing one of K lights uniformly multiplies the conditional density by 1/K. Grazing directions can make p_omega large; skipping the Jacobian is not a harmless approximation. [R23, S07]
Derive multiple importance sampling with counts intact

Let technique i contribute n_i samples from p_i. An MIS estimator is sum_i (1/n_i) sum_j w_i(X_ij) f(X_ij)/p_i(X_ij). Weights must sum to one on the covered support and vanish where the associated technique cannot sample. For the balance heuristic, w_i(x)=n_i p_i(x)/sum_k n_k p_k(x). The count terms matter when sample allocation differs. This is not the same formula as drawing one random technique and forgetting its selection probability. [S07]

Use a scalar integral as an oracle before debugging full images. For f(x)=x^2 on [0,1], I=1/3. The reference combines uniform p1=1 and p2=2x, drawing p2 samples as sqrt(U). Each strategy is weighted against both densities. Repeated seeds reveal estimation noise; one seed near 1/3 proves little by itself. Support errors and density errors should be tested deliberately.
Connect the derivation to an executable path tracer

The included CPU reference has diffuse spheres, a black environment, explicit surface-light sampling, BSDF sampling, a BVH, emission handling and balance weights. BSDF throughput for cosine-sampled Lambertian reflection simplifies to albedo. When a BSDF path reaches an emitter, the light PDF is reconstructed for the same direction so the competing contributions can be weighted consistently. [S08]

Russian roulette uses a survival probability q>0 and divides surviving throughput by q. That preserves expectation for the remaining estimator, but it does not remove the reference's separate finite-depth truncation: paths longer than six bounces are omitted. State that bias. Fixed origin offsets also depend on scene scale. Linear radiance values are saved to JSON; the PPM is a tone-mapped preview and must not be used for numerical error claims. The reference is a correctness microscope, not a real-time production renderer.
expansion.worked: For one sample from each technique, p1=2 and p2=6 give w1=2/(2+6)=0.25. With three samples from technique 1 and one from technique 2, w1=(3*2)/(3*2+1*6)=0.5. For a Lambertian surface with albedo rho under constant incoming radiance L, cosine sampling uses p=cos(theta)/pi. The contribution [rho/pi * L * cos(theta)]/p is rho*L for every nongrazing sample. With rho=0.8 and L=2, the exact reflected radiance is 1.6. This analytically checkable case catches missing pi and cosine factors.
procedure: Derive the estimator and write the probability measure beside every PDF. Include light-selection probability.
Verify the known integral and a constant-radiance Lambertian case before rendering a complex scene.
Implement or independently extend a path tracer with explicit light sampling and MIS. Compare BSDF-only, light-sampling-only and MIS variants.
Test directly visible emission, occluded lights, grazing angles, dark materials and nonuniform sample counts.
Measure error against a sufficiently converged linear-radiance reference at equal cost; retain uncertainty across seeds.
Audit finite-depth, ray-offset and reconstruction biases. Present images as supporting evidence, not the only evidence.
checks: The chosen densities cover all relevant nonzero contributions.
Area and solid-angle densities are not mixed.
MIS weights include sample counts and sum appropriately.
The reference error is characterized rather than assumed zero.
A finite-depth image is not labeled an unbiased full-transport solution.
problems: P1. Convert p_area=0.25 per square meter at distance 2 m and light cosine 0.5 to a solid-angle density.
P2. A path survives roulette with probability 0.25 and has pre-roulette contribution 3. What contribution should a surviving path carry, and what is the expectation?
solutions: P1. p_omega=0.25*4/0.5=2 per steradian. If the light was selected with probability 1/K, multiply the complete directional density by 1/K.
P2. A surviving path contributes 3/0.25=12; terminated paths contribute zero. The expectation is 0.25*12=3. This calculation concerns roulette only, not separate depth or clamping bias.

lessons.title: Real-time ray tracing, dynamic acceleration and hybrid pipelines
lessons.outcome: Budget traversal, building and shading as one system.
lessons.teach:
Ray-tracing acceleration structures trade build cost, memory and query cost. Dynamic scenes may update or rebuild structures; the best policy depends on movement, geometry and traversal degradation. A refit can be cheaper initially but leave poor bounds after large changes. Hardware-assisted traversal still needs correct synchronization and resource lifetime.
Hybrid renderers combine rasterized visibility with ray-traced shadows, reflections or indirect lighting. Each path needs a consistent material and coordinate model. Screen-space or cached approximations require fallbacks where information is absent. Measure acceleration build/update, tracing, shading, denoising and synchronization separately, then report total frame impact. Compare equivalent scene motion and image quality rather than static screenshots alone.
lessons.example: A faster traversal variant that adds 4 ms of build work to save 1 ms of tracing is a regression for a scene rebuilt every frame, but might help a scene reused for many frames.
lessons.lab: Add one ray-traced effect to the engine or build a software hybrid prototype. Pass: dynamic-scene tests include total update cost, missing-information fallbacks and resource synchronization evidence.
lessons.reading: R23: intersection acceleration and light transport; R21, R24 or R25: supported ray-tracing interfaces for an optional hardware route.

quiz.question: Why can a cheap BVH refit become a poor long-term choice?
quiz.answer: Large motion can degrade bounds and increase traversal cost.

quiz.question: Is saving 1 ms of tracing worth 4 ms of per-frame rebuild cost?
quiz.answer: Not under that stated per-frame workload; total time increases by 3 ms.

quiz.question: Why compare animated scenes?
quiz.answer: Dynamic updates and temporal behavior can dominate costs or artifacts absent in a static scene.

sections: The best acceleration structure depends on its lifetime

A hierarchy groups primitives into bounds so a ray can reject many primitives at once. A tighter or more carefully partitioned tree may cost more to build yet reduce traversal. Refit preserves topology and updates bounds after motion; rebuilding changes the partition. Evaluate total build/update plus query work over the reuse interval, not just the shortest traversal time.

For a structure rebuilt once and reused for F frames, per-frame amortized cost is build/F+trace, assuming comparable frames. That assumption can fail under motion: a cheap refit can leave broad overlapping bounds that worsen traversal. A policy should consider predicted or observed query cost, memory and update frequency. The reference uses a median-split sphere BVH rather than a sophisticated surface-area-heuristic builder, giving the learner room for a meaningful extension.
Correctness includes degenerate rays and changing geometry

A slab test intersects a ray interval against each axis-aligned box. For a zero direction component, check whether the origin lies inside that slab instead of dividing by zero. Intersections must use a consistent t interval and handle rays starting inside bounds. Compare the accelerated result against brute force for randomized rays, then test tangency, parallel rays and close surfaces explicitly.

The supplied refit assumes the same primitive identities and topology remain present. Adding or removing primitives is not covered by that operation. A dynamic-scene test should move geometry enough to change overlap and query coherence, rather than only translating the whole scene together. Track primitive tests or node visits as explanatory metrics; elapsed time alone may hide why a refit loses.
Hybrid pipelines share resources and meaning

A rasterized primary view can feed ray-traced shadows or reflections, but a ray effect must still agree about materials, coordinate frames and visibility. Screen-space information cannot describe an offscreen occluder, so a fallback must state what happens when information is missing. Do not quietly compare a screen-space approximation with full-scene rays as if they had identical quality.

Hardware acceleration adds build resources, scratch memory, device addresses, synchronization and object lifetimes. Keep source geometry and scratch allocations valid for the durations required by the API, and establish a build-write to trace-read dependency. The existence of a ray-tracing feature does not establish that every update mode or geometry change is valid. The CPU model validates intersection logic only; it does not validate those hardware lifetime requirements. [S09]
expansion.worked: Policy A takes 1 ms to refit and 5 ms to trace each frame. Policy B takes 5 ms to rebuild and 2 ms to trace. If every frame uses a fresh structure, A costs 6 ms and B costs 7 ms, so rebuilding loses. If a static structure is built once and reused for F frames, total times are 1+5F and 5+2F. B wins when 5+2F<1+5F, meaning F>4/3, so it wins from two identical-use frames onward under that simplified model. In a moving scene, the fixed 5 ms trace assumption must be retested.

Create a dynamic scene with topology-preserving movement and a separate topology-changing case requiring rebuild.
Compare refit and rebuild with the same rays and geometry snapshots. Record update, trace and total time, plus peak memory.
Integrate one hybrid shadow/reflection effect or a software equivalent with an explicit missing-information fallback.
For hardware execution, retain validation-layer output and a resource lifetime/synchronization table.
Test animated sequences and report one motion regime where the selected policy becomes worse.
checks: Accelerated and brute-force hits agree within the selected numerical tolerance.
Parallel-ray and inside-bound cases are tested.
Refit is used only under its supported topology contract.
The cost table includes updates and synchronization, not just ray traversal.
Hardware-only claims require hardware evidence.
problems: P1. Derive the break-even reuse count for two policies with build costs bA,bB and query costs qA,qB when qB<qA.
P2. Why can an animated test invalidate a conclusion obtained from a single screenshot?
solutions: P1. B wins when bB+F*qB<bA+F*qA, so F>(bB-bA)/(qA-qB). Handle nonpositive numerators separately; these assumptions exclude changing query cost during reuse.
P2. Motion changes hierarchy quality, update frequency, correspondence, resource hazards and temporal image quality. A still frame observes none of those sequence-dependent costs and failures.
expansion.reading_expanded: R23: Primitives and Intersection Acceleration; S09: Vulkan acceleration-structure specification for an optional hardware route. Follow the exact API version used by your project for build/update flags and synchronization.

lessons.title: Spatiotemporal reuse, reservoirs and denoising
lessons.outcome: Evaluate variance reduction together with bias, history validity and motion.
lessons.teach:
Temporal and spatial reuse exploit related samples across frames or nearby locations. Reusing data changes the sampling and correlation structure, so the estimator and weights must be derived rather than improvised. Reservoir sampling can retain a compact representative sample under a defined weighted selection rule; its rendering use requires additional treatment of target distributions and reuse.
Denoising reconstructs a signal from noisy observations using assumptions about spatial, temporal or learned structure. It can suppress noise while introducing bias, blur or ghosting. Visibility changes and incorrect motion vectors invalidate history. Distinguish estimator bias from reconstruction bias and assess moving sequences at equal total cost. The original 2020 ReSTIR paper is a historical reproduction option, not a claim to represent the latest technique.
lessons.example: If a moving object reveals a background, old foreground samples are not valid background evidence merely because they occupy the same pixel coordinate. History acceptance must account for correspondence and visibility.
lessons.lab: Reproduce a small weighted-reservoir example or temporal denoiser, then evaluate on motion and disocclusion sequences. Pass: the selection/weight rule is derived, bias limitations are stated and results include sequence-level failure cases.
lessons.reading: R44: original ReSTIR paper and its estimator assumptions; R23: sampling theory; read only the selected bounded method before expanding scope.

quiz.question: Why cannot reused samples always be treated as new independent samples?
quiz.answer: Reuse can introduce correlation and change the estimator's sampling structure.

quiz.question: Why is same-pixel history not enough to establish correspondence?
quiz.answer: Different surfaces can occupy that pixel after motion or disocclusion.

quiz.question: What should be compared in a denoised rendering benchmark?
quiz.answer: Quality, bias/artifacts, temporal behavior and total runtime, not only the raw ray count.

sections: Prove the weighted reservoir before reusing it

For nonnegative weights w1,...,wM, keep a running sum W and replace the current selection with item i with probability wi/W after adding its weight. Inductively, an earlier item's selection probability becomes [wj/W_old]*[W_old/W_new]=wj/W_new. The newly arrived item has probability wi/W_new. Thus the final item is selected proportionally to its weight. Reject negative and nonfinite weights. If all weights are zero, no representative is selected.

This proves a selection rule, not a rendering estimator. The reference's frequency test checks weights (1,2,7), expecting frequencies near (0.1,0.2,0.7). Statistical tolerance is declared for a fixed seed and trial count; it is not a proof of every distributional property. The all-zero case and overflow behavior are just as important as the attractive positive-weight case.
Selection weights and estimator normalization are different

Consider M independent candidates Xi~q, target surrogate p_hat positive wherever the desired contribution f is nonzero, and weights wi=p_hat(Xi)/q(Xi). After weighted selection of Y, the estimator [W/(M*p_hat(Y))]*f(Y) has conditional expectation (1/M) sum_i f(Xi)/q(Xi). Taking expectation over candidates gives the desired integral when support and integrability conditions hold. This derivation explains why keeping only Y without W and M loses essential information.

Spatial or temporal reservoir reuse changes the candidate-generation structure, the target and the correlations. Reusing a neighbor's representative as though it were a fresh draw from your proposal does not inherit the derivation above. The selected research method supplies additional normalization and validity conditions; derive those for the exact bounded variant being reproduced. Do not call a weighted reservoir implementation "ReSTIR" by itself. [R44]
History acceptance is a geometric and statistical decision

A temporal filter blends current c with reprojected history h: output=alpha*c+(1-alpha)*h for valid correspondence, otherwise output=c. The same pixel address is not correspondence when objects or the camera move. Depth, surface identity, normals, motion vectors and visibility changes can provide rejection evidence, but thresholds themselves create tradeoffs.

Noise reduction can introduce blur, lag, ghosting or estimator/reconstruction bias. Test disocclusion, a camera cut, moving highlights and changing illumination. Separate raw estimator error from reconstruction error by evaluating both before and after filtering. Sequence-level metrics and selected temporal traces expose failures that a favorable still frame hides. Total cost includes history storage, motion processing, rejection and reconstruction, not only rays saved.
expansion.worked: Suppose an old pixel is 1 and a newly revealed background is 0. With alpha=0.2 and no rejection, the filter outputs 0.8, then 0.64, then 0.512 on successive zero observations. After ten frames the remnant is 0.8^10, approximately 0.1074. The noise-free input has acquired a visible error entirely from invalid history. Correct rejection outputs 0 immediately in this simplified case. A denoiser can therefore lower static-frame noise while becoming less accurate at a visibility transition.
procedure: Derive the weighted-selection invariant and test empirical frequencies, zero weights and invalid inputs.
Either derive a bounded reservoir estimator or implement a temporal denoiser with explicit reprojection/validity rules. Do not stop at the selection class.
Construct sequences for disocclusion, a camera cut, moving geometry and lighting change. Preserve ground-truth or high-quality reference sequences.
Compare no reuse, reuse, and reuse with rejection at equal total budget; label the ablation.
Separate estimator bias, reconstruction bias, temporal error and memory/runtime costs.
For a ReSTIR reproduction, map every retained state and normalization to the selected paper equations.
checks: The selected sample probability is distinguished from the final estimator weight.
History rejection tests involve changed surfaces, not only stationary noise.
All-zero reservoirs have a defined safe outcome.
Correlation and target changes are explicitly discussed.
A complete ReSTIR claim is not made from the primitive alone.
problems: P1. For fixed candidates with weights (1,2,7), show the first item's final selection probability using the sequential replacement rule.
P2. Why is W/(M*p_hat(Y)) necessary in the simple candidate-resampling estimator, rather than outputting only f(Y)?
solutions: P1. The first item starts selected. It survives candidate 2 with probability 1/3 and candidate 3 with probability 3/10, so final probability is (1/3)*(3/10)=1/10.

P2. Y follows the weighted resampling distribution, not the original integration measure. Conditional expectation with the normalization becomes the ordinary candidate importance average. Omitting it generally integrates under the selection distribution and changes the target quantity.
