lessons.title: Differentiable and neural rendering under engineering constraints
lessons.outcome: Test learned or gradient-based methods against explicit baselines.
lessons.teach:
Differentiable rendering studies how outputs change with scene or model parameters. Visibility discontinuities, stochastic sampling and approximations complicate gradients. A useful derivative must match the actual objective and parameterization; automatic differentiation alone does not guarantee the right physical or statistical estimator. Validate on small scenes with finite differences and known cases.
Neural rendering or learned reconstruction can trade preprocessing, training and memory for runtime quality or speed. Training data coverage, scene specificity, temporal stability and inference hardware constrain deployment. Compare a non-learned baseline and include training or preprocessing cost where the claim requires it. Separate interpolation within familiar conditions from generalization to new scenes, lighting or motion.
lessons.example: A reconstruction network tested on frames from its own training sequence may perform well without generalizing to a new level. Holding out entire scenes tests a stronger claim.
lessons.lab: Implement a small inverse-rendering optimization or learned reconstruction experiment. Pass: gradient or generalization checks, a non-learned baseline, compute/memory accounting and a distribution-shift failure analysis are included.
lessons.reading: R47: automatic differentiation, optimization and generalization; R23: light transport and sampling foundations; select one original method with Module 41's paper-review protocol.

quiz.question: Does automatic differentiation guarantee the desired gradient estimator?
quiz.answer: No. The modeled computation, discontinuities and stochastic estimator must still match the intended objective.

quiz.question: Why hold out entire scenes for some rendering evaluations?
quiz.answer: It tests generalization beyond correlated frames or content seen during training.

quiz.question: When should training cost be included?
quiz.answer: When the claimed practical benefit depends on total preparation, deployment or repeated use, not only one isolated inference.

sections: Differentiate the actual inverse problem

Let observations y_i be generated by a rendering model R_i(theta). A squared-error objective is 0.5 sum_i (R_i(theta)-y_i)^2, with gradient sum_i (R_i-y_i)*dR_i/dtheta. Differentiating an implementation produces derivatives of that implementation's computational path. It does not automatically account for omitted visibility changes, discontinuous sampling choices or a mismatch between the modeled camera and the data. [S10]

Start with a smooth, identifiable subproblem: known lighting and scalar Lambertian albedo. Write R_i=rho*b_i with b_i=E*max(cos_i,0)/pi. The unconstrained optimum is rho=sum(b_i*y_i)/sum(b_i^2), projected to [0,1] for the physical albedo bound. The denominator measures sensitivity; all-dark observations provide no information about rho. The executable reference rejects that unidentifiable case instead of inventing an estimate.
Gradient checks need a noise and discontinuity policy

For deterministic smooth models, compare analytic derivatives with centered differences over a range of step sizes. For stochastic estimators, independent random samples at theta+h and theta-h can make the difference dominated by noise. Common random numbers can reduce variance when used correctly, but do not make a discontinuous or biased derivative estimator mathematically valid.

A silhouette crossing can change which surface is visible abruptly. A local derivative computed while holding the sampled path fixed may miss a boundary contribution to the desired derivative. State whether the experiment excludes visibility changes, uses an approximation or employs a method specifically designed for them. The small albedo fit deliberately keeps visibility and illumination fixed; it is a baseline, not a full differentiable renderer.
A learned method carries an additional engineering bill

For a neural route, define training inputs, targets, architecture, loss, optimizer, random seeds and stopping criterion. Hold out entire scenes when correlated frames would leak content. Compare with a non-learned baseline such as a simple temporal/spatial filter or analytic fit, not only with a deliberately undertrained network. Report training/preprocessing cost, inference time, model weights, activation memory and temporal behavior. [R47]

A preparation cost C amortized over N uses contributes C/N per use. Training can be acceptable for a repeatedly reused level yet impractical for user-generated content changed every minute. Distribution shifts include new materials, lighting, camera motion or hardware precision. Keep the performance claim limited to the tested shifts, and preserve a fallback that has a known numerical and latency contract.
expansion.worked: Let E=1, cosine values (0.2,0.5,1) and true rho=0.7. Then b=cosine/pi and y=0.7*b. The numerator of the least-squares formula is 0.7 sum(b^2), so the fitted albedo is exactly 0.7 in exact arithmetic. If you instead try to estimate both rho and unknown E from these data, only their product is observable: doubling E and halving rho leaves predictions unchanged while both remain valid. More optimizer iterations cannot remove that identifiability ambiguity; it needs a known light, a prior or additional observations.
procedure: Choose the inverse-rendering route or a bounded learned-reconstruction route; document why it fits the available compute.
For inverse rendering, derive a loss and analytic reference, check gradients and include an unidentifiable or bound-active case.
For learned reconstruction, reserve scenes, establish a non-learned baseline and record the exact training recipe and model artifact.
Evaluate a distribution shift or visibility-related failure rather than only training-like frames.
Measure preprocessing/training, inference, peak memory and temporal stability under a declared amortization horizon.
Report where the method is not trustworthy and when the engine should fall back.
checks: The optimized objective matches the claimed physical or statistical quantity.
Gradient checks or held-out generalization evidence are present.
A non-learned baseline is included.
No training-set result is presented as held-out performance.
The supplied scalar oracle is not mistaken for a trained network or full inverse renderer.
problems: P1. Derive the albedo least-squares optimum and explain what happens when all basis values are zero.
P2. A method needs 600 seconds of preparation and saves 2 milliseconds per frame. How many frames are required to break even on time alone?
solutions: P1. Set derivative sum_i b_i(rho*b_i-y_i)=0, obtaining rho=sum(b_i*y_i)/sum(b_i^2); project to [0,1] for the box-constrained scalar problem. A zero denominator means the data do not identify rho.

P2. 600/0.002=300000 frames, ignoring all other changes. At 60 frames/s that is 5000 seconds of playback, about 83.3 minutes. State whether the prepared artifact is reused across sessions and whether quality is equivalent.

modules.title: Advanced engine systems and simulation research
modules.project: Conduct an engine-system experiment with a formal model or numerical argument, a reference implementation and stress-tested integration. Choose one main depth area: world streaming, simulation, distributed state or reliability.

lessons.title: Large-world scheduling, streaming and critical-path control
lessons.outcome: Design a bounded system under changing content and workload.
lessons.teach:
Large-world engines coordinate visibility, simulation, streaming and resource residency under changing demand. A frame graph can make dependencies explicit, but hidden shared state or unpredictable tasks can still expand the critical path. Partition work by ownership and locality while controlling cross-partition communication.
World-coordinate precision can degrade far from the origin; origin rebasing, hierarchical coordinates or higher precision each affect physics, rendering and networking interfaces. Streaming priorities should reflect gameplay deadlines and resource availability, not only distance. Build a workload model with bursts, cancellation and scarce memory. Evaluate tail latency and quality degradation under stress rather than only steady travel through a preloaded scene.
lessons.example: A camera teleport invalidates a distance-based prefetch assumption and can create a sudden working-set change. The engine needs placeholders and a bounded recovery policy rather than an unlimited synchronous load.
lessons.lab: Implement a bounded world-streaming scheduler or large-coordinate experiment. Pass: teleport and memory-pressure tests preserve correctness, peak resources are measured and the critical path is explained with a trace.
lessons.reading: R26: world, task and streaming systems for comparison; R20: engine architecture; R54: numerical conditioning where coordinate precision is studied.

quiz.question: Why can a camera teleport defeat ordinary prefetching?
quiz.answer: It changes the needed content abruptly, bypassing assumptions about gradual motion.

quiz.question: Why is origin rebasing an interface issue?
quiz.answer: Physics, rendering, networking and stored references must agree on coordinate changes.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a bounded degradation policy?
quiz.answer: It limits work and resource use while explicitly choosing which quality or availability guarantees may temporarily relax.

sections: Treat streaming as admission control, not a list of loads

A request consumes more than resident asset memory. Its compressed input, decompression scratch, decoded output, upload staging and temporary old version may overlap in lifetime. Define separate budgets and the ownership of each reservation. Admission should account for the peak overlap, not only the final asset size. A bounded queue prevents unbounded metadata growth; a resident-byte limit does not by itself bound pending allocations.

Assign a deadline, priority, estimated cost and cancellation identity to each request. Distance may predict demand during ordinary travel, but a teleport defeats that prediction. A policy can retain a low-detail representation, refuse low-priority work or show a placeholder while recovering. Those are deliberate quality/availability changes. Blocking the frame until every missing asset arrives is also a policy, usually with a very different latency contract.
The frame deadline follows dependencies

Represent frame tasks as a directed acyclic graph. Its critical path is the longest dependency chain, including synchronization and required data movement. Adding workers cannot remove a serial dependency. A background task can still delay the frame through a shared allocator lock, memory pressure or a mandatory join. Instrument readiness, queue wait, service, completion and consumption separately rather than timing only the task body.

An epoch identifies a world request generation. On teleport, increment the epoch and cancel obsolete work. A late completion must check its epoch before publishing a resource; cancellation cannot assume that a device operation already in flight instantly stops. Publication and resource retirement need explicit lifetime rules. The supplied model clears queued requests on epoch changes, but implementing late asynchronous completions is a required lab extension, not an already tested feature.
Large coordinates cross subsystem boundaries

In a binary floating-point format, absolute spacing grows with the magnitude of a coordinate. A single-precision value near 2^20 has spacing 2^(20-23)=0.125 in its represented units. Millimeter-level changes cannot all be represented there. A local origin or cell-plus-offset representation separates large world location from fine local motion; merely switching one render variable to double precision does not synchronize physics, networking and saved references.

Define which coordinate space every interface accepts. During rebasing, preserve object identity and transform histories consistently, including previous-frame positions used for motion vectors. Test transitions across cell boundaries and the origin shift during outstanding streaming work. Preserve a stable world-space identity for persistence; a temporary local coordinate should not become the sole database key.
expansion.worked: Suppose the frame needs CPU tasks A=2 ms, B=3 ms after A, and C=4 ms after A, followed by D=1 ms after both B and C. Total work is 10 ms, but the ideal critical path is A+C+D=7 ms. With two workers and no other costs, 7 ms is attainable; dividing total work by two and claiming 5 ms ignores dependencies. If D additionally waits for a 5 ms upload started only after C, the path grows to 12 ms. Moving the upload to a background queue does not remove the dependency if D still needs its result.
procedure: Draw an engine streaming state machine and a frame dependency graph. Declare queue, resident, scratch and staging budgets.
Run the supplied bounded model, then add late completions tagged by epoch and an explicit reservation lifecycle.
Inject a teleport while work is pending, oversize assets, repeated cancellations, queue saturation and memory pressure.
Add a cell-plus-local-coordinate experiment or a rebase trace that includes previous-frame transforms.
Record maximum outstanding requests, peak bytes, deadline misses and recovery time; classify placeholders as deliberate degradation.
Connect at least one measured/model trace to the critical path and label which time values are analytical rather than device measurements.
checks: Resident memory and transient overlap are separately bounded.
An obsolete completion cannot publish into the new world epoch.
Every accepted request ends in completion, rejection or cancellation under the stated progress assumptions.
The trace includes a teleport and a scarce-memory case.
Coordinate conventions are explicit at physics/render/network boundaries.
problems: P1. What is the ideal critical path of A=2, B=3 after A, C=4 after A and D=1 after B and C? Can four workers reduce it?
P2. A resident budget is 100 MB, existing assets use 70 MB and a new 20 MB asset needs 25 MB of overlapping scratch/staging. Does a final-residency-only check safely admit it?
solutions: P1. 7 ms through A,C,D. Four workers do not shorten these dependencies; improving the algorithm or overlap is required.

P2. Final residency would be 90 MB, but overlapping memory is 115 MB if charged to the same physical budget. Admission must reserve transient bytes or defer/evict safely. Separate budgets still require a combined physical-memory feasibility check.

lessons.title: Deformable simulation, variational models and solver tradeoffs
lessons.outcome: Derive a physical or constraint model before comparing visual results.
lessons.teach:
Deformable simulation represents degrees of freedom and a model of forces, energies or constraints. Spatial discretization, boundary conditions and time integration together define the numerical problem. Finite-element or mass-spring approaches approximate different structures; a visually similar result does not prove equivalent material behavior.
Implicit methods can improve stability for stiff systems while requiring nonlinear or linear solves and introducing other errors. Position-based and compliant-constraint methods offer alternative formulations with their own parameters and convergence behavior. Derive one simple energy or constraint, explain its units and study timestep/iteration sensitivity. Separate stability, accuracy and physical fidelity. A stable method can be inaccurate, and an accurate local solver can still use an inappropriate material model.
lessons.example: For spring energy E=0.5*k*(x-rest)^2, the force is -dE/dx=-k*(x-rest). This derivative supplies a check before extending to a multi-particle system.
lessons.lab: Implement a small cloth, elastic bar or compliant-constraint model and compare two integration/solver choices. Pass: derive the core equations, check gradients, quantify constraint or energy error and reproduce one bounded result from the assigned research.
lessons.reading: R54: equilibrium, variational and differential-equation methods; R55: 2016 XPBD and related position-based simulation course notes.

quiz.question: What force follows from the example spring energy?
quiz.answer: -k*(x-rest).

quiz.question: Does numerical stability guarantee physical accuracy?
quiz.answer: No. A stable trajectory can still have large discretization error or use an unsuitable physical model.

quiz.question: Why vary timestep and solver iterations independently?
quiz.answer: They affect different sources of error and can reveal hidden parameter dependence.

sections: Start from energy, mass and a time discretization

For a one-dimensional spring displacement C(x)=x-rest, energy is E=0.5*k*C^2 and force is -k*C. If k has units N/m, compliance alpha=1/k has units m/N. A multi-particle constraint has gradients with respect to every participating position and inverse masses that govern how a correction is distributed. A pinned particle has inverse mass zero; it must not move under the constraint correction.

For implicit Euler on a linear spring system with mass matrix M, stiffness K and step h, eliminating velocity gives (M+h^2*K)*x_next=M*(x+h*v)+h^2*f, with rest offsets incorporated consistently in the force or displacement formulation. This is a numerical approximation to the dynamics, not the exact continuous trajectory. An independently assembled dense solution is a useful oracle for a small sparse/iterative implementation.
Derive compliant projection and preserve the multiplier

XPBD introduces scaled compliance alpha_tilde=alpha/h^2. For one constraint, the multiplier increment is delta_lambda=(-C-alpha_tilde*lambda)/(sum_i w_i*||grad_i C||^2+alpha_tilde). Positions receive delta_x_i=w_i*grad_i C*delta_lambda. Accumulate lambda across solver iterations within the step; resetting it at every iteration changes the method. The simple reference resets it at each new timestep and retains it across that timestep's iterations. [S05]

For a scalar unit-mass constraint with alpha=0.01, h=0.1 and predicted displacement 1, alpha_tilde=1. Starting lambda=0 gives delta_lambda=-1/(1+1)=-0.5, so the corrected displacement is 0.5. The accumulated lambda is -0.5 and the constraint-plus-compliance residual is 0.5+1*(-0.5)=0. An extra identical iteration makes no change. This is compliant equilibrium for the step, not a failed attempt to enforce C=0.
Separate model, discretization and solve error

A simulation has at least three distinct error sources: the chosen physical model, time/space discretization and incomplete numerical solution. Changing iterations primarily changes solve error. Changing h changes the discrete time problem as well as alpha_tilde. Changing mesh spacing without rescaling material parameters can change the represented physical material. Vary these independently and compare at equal simulated time.

The executable bar is a pinned one-dimensional chain of unit-mass displacements with linear neighboring springs. Its converged XPBD result can be compared with a separately assembled implicit-Euler solve of the same discrete problem. It is not a three-dimensional cloth implementation, collision solver or general nonlinear finite-element model. Use its agreement as a stepping stone to a bounded paper result; do not generalize it to all deformable simulation. Stable pictures alone do not establish accurate forces, constraint errors or material behavior.
expansion.worked: For the scalar values above, resetting lambda to zero on each iteration produces x=0.5, then 0.25, then 0.125. The solver incorrectly drives a compliant spring toward a hard constraint as iterations increase. Keeping lambda gives x=0.5 after the first iteration and thereafter. This one-variable counterexample isolates the role of multiplier accumulation more clearly than a cloth screenshot. Use the reset-every-iteration variant as an explicitly incorrect ablation, not as an alternative implementation of XPBD.
procedure: Derive the scalar spring force, implicit-Euler equation and XPBD update with units and mass weighting.
Run the scalar oracle and the bar sensitivity experiment. Check pinned boundaries and zero initial displacement.
Compare iterative XPBD with the independent dense solve at identical timestep, material parameters, forcing and simulated duration.
Vary timestep and iteration count independently; add a material/stiffness sweep and report residual/error, not only runtime.
Reproduce a bounded result or property from S05 with its assumptions mapped to your implementation. Add one honest extension, such as ordering or stiffness sensitivity.
Document stability, numerical accuracy and physical-model limitations separately; avoid claiming energy conservation for a dissipative implicit method.
checks: Compliance scales with h squared as specified by the selected formulation.
Multipliers accumulate within a timestep.
Reference and candidate solve the same discrete problem.
The physical duration remains constant across timestep sweeps.
A paper reproduction is distinguished from a scalar teaching oracle.
problems: P1. Compute the first and second scalar updates for w=1, C=1 initially, alpha=0.01 and h=0.1 with accumulated multipliers.
P2. If a timestep is halved while physical compliance is held fixed, how does alpha_tilde change? Does this alone prove that trajectories at the two timesteps match?
solutions: P1. alpha_tilde=1, delta_lambda=-0.5, x=0.5 and lambda=-0.5. The second numerator is -0.5-1*(-0.5)=0, so no further update occurs.

P2. alpha_tilde increases by a factor of four. This preserves the intended compliance scaling in the formulation but does not eliminate time-discretization, collision, nonlinear or finite-iteration differences. Compare at equal physical time and convergence criteria.

lessons.title: Distributed game state, consistency and overload behavior
lessons.outcome: Specify which guarantees survive network delay and partial failure.
lessons.teach:
Distributed engine services divide state across processes or machines. Some operations require a single authoritative order, while others tolerate delayed or approximate views. Consistency is a property of a specified operation and model, not a single adjective that applies equally to every subsystem. During communication failure, availability and agreement requirements can conflict.
Partition ownership, migration and recovery need explicit protocols. A world handoff must not create two authorities granting the same irreversible outcome. Queues require bounds and backpressure; retry storms can magnify overload. Test fault sequences involving delayed messages, crashes and duplicate requests. Use local process simulation before public infrastructure, and never claim internet-scale behavior from a two-process happy-path demo.
lessons.example: If two servers both accept ownership of the same entity during a failed handoff, both might award a unique item. A versioned ownership or fencing mechanism must prevent stale authority from committing that effect.
lessons.lab: Model a two-partition entity handoff with injected failure. Pass: a stated safety invariant holds, recovery assumptions are explicit and overload is bounded without unbounded retry amplification.
lessons.reading: R17-R18: transport and transactions; R20: game-state architecture; use Module 41's claim and experiment discipline for the distributed model.

quiz.question: Why is duplicate authority dangerous?
quiz.answer: Two participants may both commit effects that should occur only once under one owner.

quiz.question: What is a retry storm?
quiz.answer: Many failed or slow requests trigger additional retries that worsen overload.

quiz.question: Can a small local demo establish internet-scale reliability?
quiz.answer: No. It supports only the tested model and scale unless broader evidence is provided.

sections: Specify the operation that requires authority

A position snapshot may tolerate delay while granting a unique item requires an unambiguous committed decision. Define operations, their observable effects and the consistency requirement of each. A server believing it owns an entity is not sufficient when old messages can arrive after ownership changes. The receiver that commits an irreversible effect must enforce the ownership rule.

A fencing token is a monotonically advancing ownership epoch checked by that committing receiver. After epoch 8 replaces epoch 7, an epoch-7 request must be rejected even if its sender still believes its lease is valid. The transfer of ownership itself needs a correctly coordinated, durable protocol in a real distributed system. The teaching model assumes a single atomic store that updates authority and checks commits; it does not implement replicated consensus or survive an actual machine power loss. [S11, S17]
Make duplicate handling part of the transaction

An accepted operation needs an idempotency identity and a recorded result. If a client times out after the server commits, its retry must not repeat the effect. Check the request ID, validate its payload consistency, apply the effect and record its result atomically relative to competing operations. A repeated ID with a different payload is a conflict, not a free new request.

Deduplication storage is finite. Expiring an ID without a declared retry horizon can make a very late duplicate appear new. Keeping every ID forever is an unbounded resource promise. State a retention/epoch policy or reject new work when the bounded educational store fills. Exactly-once effects require a specified boundary and failure model; a transport protocol's delivery behavior does not by itself guarantee the application's transaction semantics.
Test histories, not just individual error codes

A useful fault schedule is: old owner sends a request, the request is delayed, ownership transfers, new owner commits, the delayed old request arrives, then a retry is duplicated. Check the complete committed history and invariant, not only whether each function returned a plausible status. Introduce crashes before and after the imagined commit boundary to expose what must be persisted.

Under overload, bound ingress queues, outstanding requests and retries. Backoff with jitter can reduce synchronization, but a retry budget and deadline are still needed to stop unlimited amplification. Distinguish rejection, timeout and unknown commit outcome. Test the recovery path when the deduplication capacity is exhausted. Local deterministic schedules are excellent semantic tests; they are not measurements of internet latency or evidence of global service reliability.
expansion.worked: Owner A holds epoch 7. Its award request is delayed. Authority changes atomically to B at epoch 8; B commits award request R. When A's epoch-7 operation reaches the authoritative sink, the sink rejects it before applying an effect. A retry of B's same request R returns its recorded result without re-awarding. Without the sink's epoch check, a correct-looking handoff acknowledgment cannot stop A's delayed request from committing. Without atomic deduplication, two simultaneous copies of R could both pass a separate check and award twice.
procedure: State one safety invariant, the commit boundary, ownership-transfer assumptions and what is durably recorded.
Run the fenced-store tests and draw the history of a delayed old-owner request.
Build a two-partition local process or deterministic event simulation with delay, duplication, timeout and restart events.
Test same-ID/same-payload retries, same-ID/conflicting-payload requests, stale epochs and deduplication capacity exhaustion.
Add bounded retries and backpressure; quantify offered work versus accepted work during a retry burst.
Write a limitations section explaining what a production consensus/storage layer must provide beyond the teaching store.
checks: Stale authority is rejected where the irreversible effect commits.
Duplicate detection and the effect share an atomic boundary in the stated model.
Queue and deduplication growth are bounded.
Safety is tested across a failure sequence rather than only a happy path.
Durability, scale and network claims do not exceed the tested model.
problems: P1. Why is a lease on the sending server insufficient to reject a delayed stale write at an external sink?
P2. A request can be retried three times after its original attempt. What is the maximum attempt amplification for one logical request, and why is that not a sufficient overload policy alone?
solutions: P1. The sink may receive an old request after authority has moved; the old sender may also be paused or partitioned. A monotonic epoch checked by the sink, with correctly coordinated ownership and persistence assumptions, prevents that stale operation from committing.
P2. Four attempts per logical request. Many simultaneous clients can still exceed capacity; deadlines, admission limits, bounded outstanding requests and controlled retry timing are also needed.

lessons.title: Formal specifications, replay and reliability-oriented engine design
lessons.outcome: Use precise invariants to reduce the space of subtle failures.
lessons.teach:
A formal model abstracts a system to states and transitions so properties can be examined precisely. Safety states that something bad never happens; liveness states that something good eventually happens under assumptions. An engine resource manager can have safety invariants about ownership and liveness obligations about eventual completion or cancellation.
Model checking explores the chosen abstraction, not every detail of the production implementation. Connect model transitions to real code and tests. Deterministic replay, fault injection and property-based testing complement formal reasoning by exercising implemented behavior. Avoid vacuous proofs from impossible environment assumptions. A reliability claim should identify the property, model, bound and implementation evidence separately.
lessons.example: For an asset request, safety might require that a released owner never receives a callback touching its memory. Liveness might require that each accepted request eventually completes or cancels, assuming the worker continues to run.
lessons.lab: Model a small engine lifecycle or queue protocol and connect it to implementation tests. Pass: at least one safety and one conditional liveness property are defined, a deliberate violation is found and abstraction limits are documented.
lessons.reading: R50: safety, liveness and assumptions as a formal-methods reference; R11 and Module 18: ownership/concurrency contracts; R26: system comparison.

quiz.question: How do safety and liveness differ?
quiz.answer: Safety excludes forbidden events; liveness requires eventual progress under stated assumptions.

quiz.question: Why must liveness assumptions mention scheduling or worker progress?
quiz.answer: An environment that never lets work run can prevent completion regardless of the local algorithm.

quiz.question: Does proving an abstract model automatically prove all implementation code?
quiz.answer: No. The relationship between the model and implementation must be established and checked.

sections: Define states and transitions before selecting a prover

A formal specification starts with variables, allowed initial states and a transition relation. For an asset request, useful state includes owner-alive, request-issued, request-pending and whether an invalid callback occurred. State the invariant: a callback must not touch an owner after release. A transition that completes pending work must check owner validity or use a lifetime mechanism that guarantees the target still exists.

Safety says that forbidden behavior never occurs. A finite bad prefix can demonstrate a safety violation. Liveness instead demands eventual progress, such as each accepted request eventually completing or being canceled. A model that allows the worker to be ignored forever cannot promise completion without a scheduling or fairness assumption. Fairness is a substantive environment requirement, not a magic word added after the proof. [S12]
A finite model can be complete for itself and incomplete for the engine

Breadth-first search of all reachable states is exhaustive for a finite model when its transition relation and initial states are fully represented. Store predecessor edges to recover a minimal-step counterexample. The supplied one-request model explores this graph and deliberately disables the callback guard to expose the sequence request, release, complete. Passing the guarded model says nothing by itself about arbitrary request counts, memory reclamation, real pointers or device callbacks.

Connect each model transition to code and an implementation test. Check that assumptions do not eliminate the very failures you intend to study. For example, declaring release impossible while work is pending would make the ownership test vacuous if real callers can release then. Mutation testing helps: a deliberately missing guard must produce a counterexample, proving that the checked property can detect the intended class of mistake.
Replay preserves evidence only when nondeterminism is captured

A seed alone is not always a replay record. Input order, clock reads, external responses, thread scheduling, floating-point environment and random-number consumption can affect results. Define which nondeterminism is recorded, controlled or excluded. Hash canonical serialized states at checkpoints and compare the first divergence, but retain the underlying state or event log so a mismatch is diagnosable.

The reference hash sorts JSON object keys and uses a stable digest; it is not a cross-platform floating-point determinism guarantee or a cryptographic proof of correct simulation. Replay and fault injection complement model checking by exercising actual code. Keep the evidence labels separate: model safety, conditional liveness argument, implementation tests and measured reliability are different claims.
expansion.worked: Start with alive=true and no pending request. The request transition sets pending=true. Release sets alive=false. In the buggy model, complete unconditionally dispatches the callback, setting bad=true. The resulting three-transition trace is a safety counterexample. In the guarded model, complete clears pending but does not call the dead owner. This fixes the stated safety property. It does not prove liveness: a scheduler that never executes complete or cancel can leave pending=true forever. A progress assumption and separate liveness analysis are required.
procedure: Specify a small lifecycle or queue model with state variables, initial states, transitions and one safety property.
State a separate conditional liveness requirement and its fairness/resource assumptions.
Run the finite-state safety checker and reproduce the deliberate missing-guard counterexample.
Add a realistic feature such as a second request, generation reuse or cancellation acknowledgment; report state-space size and bounds.
Map model transitions to implementation tests and create a deterministic event replay with checkpoint state comparisons.
Explain which properties were exhaustively checked, tested, argued informally or not evaluated.
checks: The deliberate bug is detected, preventing a vacuous passing result.
Safety and liveness are not conflated.
The environment assumptions permit realistic cancellation/release races.
At least one counterexample is connected to a concrete code test.
Replay records enough nondeterminism for the claimed execution model.
problems: P1. Does exhaustive safety exploration of the supplied one-request model establish eventual completion? Explain.
P2. Why should an artifact keep event/state data as well as their hashes?
solutions: P1. No. Eventual completion is a liveness property; the model may permit infinite stuttering or starvation. It requires explicit progress assumptions and a separate liveness check or argument. Exhaustiveness is relative to the finite safety model.
P2. A hash locates disagreement but does not explain it. Event and state data allow inspection of the first differing input, schedule or field and make replay failures actionable.

lessons.title: Intermediate representations, SSA and dataflow analysis
lessons.outcome: Represent program meaning so transformations can be justified.
lessons.teach:
An intermediate representation makes control flow, values and operations explicit. Static single assignment gives each value one defining assignment; merge points use a representation such as phi nodes to select values from predecessor paths. SSA simplifies many analyses but does not by itself establish program correctness.
Dataflow analysis computes properties over a control-flow graph, often through iterative fixed points on a chosen domain. Liveness identifies values that may be used later; constant propagation tracks values known under the analysis. Soundness means the analysis does not exclude behavior relevant to its guarantee, while precision controls how much useful information it retains. Dominance and control-flow edges must remain consistent after transformations.
lessons.example: After an if/else assigning x=1 or x=2, a merge can represent x=phi(1 from then, 2 from else). Replacing it with 1 unconditionally would be wrong unless the else path is proven unreachable.
lessons.lab: Extend the tiny compiler with a control-flow IR and one dataflow analysis. Pass: derive transfer functions and a fixed-point stopping condition, test loops and merges, and verify transformed programs against an interpreter.
lessons.reading: R14: LLVM frontend, control flow and optimization tutorials; R48: compiler/architecture interaction.

quiz.question: What does SSA require of each value?
quiz.answer: One defining assignment in the representation.

quiz.question: Why is the example phi node not always constant 1?
quiz.answer: The else predecessor supplies 2 unless that path is proven unreachable.

quiz.question: What is the role of a fixed point in dataflow analysis?
quiz.answer: It marks a state where further propagation under the analysis rules no longer changes the computed facts.

sections: SSA is an explicit representation of alternatives

In static single assignment form, each value name has one definition. A control-flow merge selects a value from a predecessor through a phi node. The choice follows the edge actually taken; it is not an eager evaluation of both branches. For a loop, a header phi can choose the initial value on entry and the updated value on the backedge. Dominance requires a definition to be available on every path to an ordinary use; phi inputs have edge-specific rules. [S13]

Changing control-flow edges requires updating phi predecessors and preserving dominance. A transformation that deletes a branch but leaves an obsolete phi input is not a harmless formatting issue. In a loop with multiple phis, all incoming values are selected from the predecessor environment together; assigning them sequentially can accidentally make one phi read another's new value rather than the old edge value.
Dataflow is a fixed-point computation over a chosen abstraction

For backward liveness, OUT[B] is the union of IN sets for successor blocks and IN[B]=USE[B] union (OUT[B] minus DEF[B]). Iterate until no set changes. On a finite variable universe, a monotone formulation starting from empty sets reaches a fixed point. This computes conservative possible future uses, not the exact concrete values of every execution.

In SSA, phi operands are uses on specific incoming edges. A generic block-level liveness routine without phi-aware edge treatment needs preprocessing or extension. The included live_variables function uses an explicit ordinary USE/DEF/successor input contract; do not silently feed it phi semantics it does not implement. Work-list scheduling changes the number of iterations, not the intended least fixed point of this monotone framework.
An interpreter is a differential-testing anchor

Define integer width, overflow, branch interpretation, unsupported operations and the step limit of the reference interpreter. The supplied CFG executes unsigned 32-bit arithmetic modulo 2^32 and has a fuel limit so a malformed or nonterminating student program does not run forever. It handles branches, loop phis and bounded execution, but does not statically prove unique definitions, full dominance or type consistency for every possible IR.

Before optimizing, add a verifier for the subset you accept. Then compare original and transformed programs over directed boundary values and randomized inputs. A concrete differential test can find a bug; it does not replace a legality argument for all inputs. Preserve both the IR before/after and a minimal failing input when the comparison disagrees.
expansion.worked: Consider an if/else that yields a=1 on the then edge and b=2 on the else edge. The merge is x=phi(then:a, else:b). With a runtime condition, the abstract constant result is not known to be 1. If constant propagation proves the condition true, it may remove the else edge and replace the phi by a, after repairing the CFG. For liveness, if a later block uses x, x is live into that block; the corresponding incoming operand is live only on the edge that supplies it in a phi-aware analysis.
procedure: Write the accepted IR grammar, type rules, arithmetic contract, terminators and phi edge semantics.
Run the CFG examples and add a diamond merge, counted loop and simultaneous-phi swap case.
Derive liveness transfer functions and implement a work-list analysis; document phi preprocessing or implement edge-aware uses.
Add at least one static verifier check beyond runtime execution, such as predecessor/phi agreement or dominance for ordinary uses.
Implement a transformation such as proven-branch simplification or constant propagation, preserving before/after IR.
Differential-test interpreter results and explain termination of the analysis separately from termination of the program.
checks: Phi values are selected by the actual predecessor and assigned simultaneously.
Loops and merges are covered, not only straight-line expressions.
The dataflow domain, transfer rules and fixed point are stated.
A failed verifier rejects invalid IR before optimization.
No full compiler-verification claim is made from a bounded interpreter.
problems: P1. For USE[B]={a}, DEF[B]={b}, OUT[B]={b,c}, compute IN[B].
P2. Two loop phis swap x and y on a backedge. Why must their incoming values be selected simultaneously?
solutions: P1. IN[B]={a} union ({b,c} minus {b})={a,c}.
P2. Both phis must read the predecessor values. Sequentially updating x before reading it for y can duplicate a value instead of swapping, violating the edge semantics.

lessons.title: Alias analysis, vectorization and legal optimization
lessons.outcome: Separate transformations that are fast from transformations that preserve meaning.
lessons.teach:
An optimization must preserve the language's permitted observable behavior under its assumptions. Alias analysis determines which references may identify overlapping storage. Incorrectly assuming no aliasing can make loop reordering or vectorization wrong. Undefined behavior, overflow rules and floating-point options affect what transformations are legal, so record the compilation contract.
Vectorization groups iterations only when dependencies and semantics permit it. Reductions, exceptional values and rounding can require special handling. Register allocation maps values to a limited physical register set; spills introduce memory traffic. Inspect generated code and test adversarial inputs. A faster compiler output that silently changes required results is a correctness failure, not an optimization.
lessons.example: For a[i]=a[i-1]+1, iterations depend on previous results. Treating all iterations as independent changes behavior unless a valid alternative algorithm preserves the recurrence.
lessons.lab: Implement or study a loop transformation with an explicit legality check. Pass: overlapping-memory and boundary cases are tested, compiler flags are recorded and speed claims exclude transformations that violate the required numerical contract.
lessons.reading: R14: optimization and code generation; R11: aliasing, lifetime and arithmetic guidance; R37: vector/parallel execution consequences.

quiz.question: Why is alias analysis important for reordering loads and stores?
quiz.answer: Two apparently different references may access the same storage, creating dependencies.

quiz.question: Are iterations of a[i]=a[i-1]+1 independent?
quiz.answer: No. Each depends on the previous result.

quiz.question: Why record floating-point compiler options?
quiz.answer: They can permit transformations that change rounding, exceptional-value handling or other required semantics.

sections: Legality comes before profitability

A transformation is legal only if it preserves the permitted observable behavior under its declared language contract. For unsigned 32-bit arithmetic, additions and multiplications wrap modulo 2^32. Algebraic identities valid in that ring can justify constant folding. Signed overflow, floating-point reassociation and exception behavior obey different rules; do not reuse a proof across those contracts without checking the assumptions.

The reference native example checks (x+0)*(2+3) against x*5 for 100,000 unsigned inputs and has a simple algebraic justification. Those tests support implementation confidence; the ring identity supplies the all-input argument. Converting the example to a floating-point expression with NaN, infinities or signed zero can invalidate identities that seemed obvious over real numbers. [S13]
Alias and dependence facts constrain the schedule

Two syntactically different references can denote overlapping storage. A write through one reference may change what a later read through another observes. Before reordering, distinguish true data dependence, anti-dependence and output dependence. A loop-carried recurrence such as a[i]=a[i-1]+1 cannot simply be evaluated as independent lanes.

For half-open logical ranges [a,a+n) and [b,b+m), overlap exists when a<b+m and b<a+n, provided both lengths are positive. The reference models integer offsets. Native pointer ordering/provenance and overflow-safe address arithmetic require additional language-specific care. A runtime range check can dispatch to a vectorized no-overlap path and a conservative fallback, but a false no-alias annotation does not make overlapping inputs legal. [S15]
Inspect the complete generated computation

Request optimization remarks and inspect generated assembly or intermediate code for the actual target. An optimization may add a runtime alias guard, scalar remainder loop, gathers, conversions or spills. Count the effect on the calling workload, not just one attractive vector instruction. Short loops may spend more time dispatching than computing.

Keep semantic tests active in optimized builds. The native reference uses explicit checks rather than assertions that disappear under common Release settings. Run sanitizers separately from timing; instrumentation changes execution cost. Sweep aligned, unaligned, overlapping where permitted, empty and remainder sizes. Reject any speed result that violates the required numerical or memory contract.
expansion.worked: Let a initially be [7,0,0,0] and apply a[i]=a[i-1]+1 for i=1,2,3 in order. The result is [7,8,9,10]. A naive simultaneous implementation that reads all original previous elements gives [7,8,1,1]. There may be a valid alternative algorithm for this particular recurrence, but proving and implementing that algorithm is different from asserting that the original iterations are independent. The adversarial initial values make the hidden dependence obvious.
procedure: Select a loop or expression transformation and write an explicit arithmetic/aliasing contract.
Prove its legality for the accepted subset; list the cases that require a fallback.
Add boundary, overlapping-memory and exceptional-value tests appropriate to that contract.
Build the C++ reference in Debug and Release, then run a separate sanitizer configuration on a supported compiler.
Capture optimizer remarks and generated code for at least two workload sizes; identify guards, tails and spills where present.
Measure end-to-end impact with checks outside the timed region and output consumption that prevents dead-code elimination.
checks: Numerical equivalence is required before speed is considered.
No-alias assumptions match actual caller behavior.
Remainders and short loops are tested.
The exact compiler flags and target are recorded.
Sanitizer timings are not mixed with release performance measurements.
problems: P1. Do the half-open logical ranges [0,8) and [8,16) overlap? What about [0,8) and [7,9)?
P2. Why does a passing randomized test suite not by itself prove an optimization legal for every input?
solutions: P1. The first pair does not overlap because the shared endpoint is excluded from the first range. The second pair overlaps on [7,8). Zero-length ranges overlap nothing.

P2. It samples a finite subset and may miss rare values, aliases or control-flow paths. A semantic argument states why all accepted inputs preserve behavior; tests check that the implementation follows that argument.
expansion.reading_expanded: S13: LLVM language semantics; S15: LLVM loop and SLP vectorizers; R11: lifetime, arithmetic and aliasing contracts. Record actual compiler versions and flags, not an assumed universal optimizer behavior.

lessons.title: Domain-specific languages, specialization and safe JIT execution
lessons.outcome: Trade generality for predictable game-engine computation.
lessons.teach:
A domain-specific language restricts expression to make authoring, validation or optimization easier. A material graph, particle formula or animation expression can expose structure that a general compiler cannot easily infer. Define types, allowed effects and resource limits before implementing code generation.
Specialization precomputes decisions known from material or scene parameters, potentially reducing runtime branches at the cost of more variants and compilation work. Just-in-time compilation introduces startup latency, code-cache management and execution-security concerns. Cache keys must include meaningful inputs and tool versions. Untrusted scripts or graphs need capability and complexity limits. A restricted interpreter remains a useful fallback and semantic reference.
lessons.example: Specializing four binary material options can create up to 2^4=16 variants before other parameters are considered. Uncontrolled variant growth can increase build time and runtime cache misses.
lessons.lab: Build a typed expression or material DSL with constant folding and a bounded interpreter or JIT route. Pass: invalid graphs fail safely, variant counts are measured and compiled outputs match the reference.
lessons.reading: R14: language implementation and JIT; R26: material and scripting concepts for comparison; Module 20: trust boundaries.

quiz.question: How many combinations do four independent binary options create?
Why limit the effects allowed in a DSL?
quiz.answer: Restrictions make validation, optimization and safe execution more tractable.

quiz.question: Why keep an interpreter alongside compiled execution?
quiz.answer: It provides a portable fallback and a simpler reference for semantic testing.

sections: Restrict the language to make its contract testable

A useful game-engine DSL may express a material formula, particle update or animation parameter rather than an arbitrary program. Define its types, effects, evaluation order and resource limits. The supplied expression language accepts unsigned 32-bit constants, named inputs, addition and multiplication. It forbids filesystem, network, calls, dynamic imports and arbitrary evaluation. Trees are validated before interpretation or code generation.

Node-count and depth limits bound the work of this tree interpreter. Inputs are range-checked. Generated input names come from a controlled identifier mapping rather than pasting user strings directly into C++ source. These controls reduce the accepted language's risk and simplify optimization, but they are not an operating-system isolation boundary. Untrusted native code still needs a separate security design.
Specialization trades runtime work for variants

A constant material option can remove a runtime branch or fold a subexpression. With k independent binary options, there can be 2^k combinations before considering formats, lighting modes or targets. Not every combination needs eager compilation. Use a bounded cache, compilation budget, prioritized common variants and a reference fallback for misses.

The cache key must include all semantic inputs: source graph, specialization parameters, target, arithmetic flags, ABI/schema and relevant compiler version. Omitting a target feature or floating-point option can make an old binary appear valid under a new contract. Record cache hits, misses, compile latency, peak bytes and eviction behavior rather than measuring only warmed execution.
Keep code generation separate from permission to execute

The interpreter is the semantic reference and portable fallback. Constant folding must validate its input and preserve the unsigned arithmetic contract. Generated C++ should be inspected and tested against the interpreter for a bounded trusted corpus. Native compilation is an optional extension; no raw graph should cause the package to invoke a shell with user-controlled text.

A real JIT must additionally manage executable memory, code lifetime during concurrent use, cancellation, target capabilities and isolation. Writable/executable memory policies are one part of the design, not a complete sandbox. Process boundaries, capabilities, resource quotas and trusted compiler/runtime components may be needed depending on the threat model. The supplied code deliberately stops at restricted interpretation and source generation so it does not imply those protections have been implemented. [S16]
expansion.worked: Eight binary material options allow 256 variants. At 80 KiB of code per variant, eagerly retaining all of them consumes 20,480 KiB, exactly 20 MiB, before metadata or other target variants. At 12 ms of compilation per variant, serial eager compilation adds 3.072 seconds. Specializing only the 20 common combinations initially reduces the immediate code budget to about 1.56 MiB and compilation to 240 ms, while uncommon cases use the fallback or a bounded later compilation path. Whether this improves the game depends on actual option frequencies and latency constraints.
procedure: Specify DSL grammar, type/effect rules, node/depth limits and arithmetic behavior.
Implement a learner interpreter and compare it with the reference on valid and invalid trees.
Add constant folding and verify original-versus-folded results for boundary values and randomized inputs.
Generate a bounded trusted C++ corpus or extend your existing compiler; never use eval or shell interpolation to execute graph text.
Implement or model a variant cache with complete keys, a size bound and an explicit miss fallback.
Document compilation/execution trust boundaries and the protections still required for a real untrusted JIT.
checks: Invalid trees and oversized inputs fail before execution.
The language has an explicit effects policy.
Cache keys include target, compiler and semantic flags.
Cold-start and cache behavior are measured or explicitly modeled.
Restricted interpretation is not described as an operating-system sandbox.
problems: P1. How many combinations result from eight independent binary options, and what happens after adding two more?
P2. Why can a cache key based only on source text be incorrect after a compiler or target change?
solutions: P1. 2^8=256. Ten options produce 1024, a fourfold increase. Runtime frequencies and resource limits should guide which variants are materialized.

P2. Identical source can compile under different semantics, ABIs or target capabilities. The cached result may be incompatible or wrong unless those inputs and relevant tool versions are part of its identity.

lessons.title: Compiler/hardware co-design and graduate artifact review
lessons.outcome: Connect a transformation to architecture and application evidence.
lessons.teach:
Compiler decisions influence memory layout, instruction mix, register demand and parallel scheduling. Hardware features are useful only when software can express and exploit them efficiently. A co-design experiment changes one interface, representation or instruction opportunity and measures its complete effect. Avoid attributing a gain to hardware when it actually comes from a stronger software baseline.
Graduate review requires a defensible claim, mathematical or semantic argument, implementation and reproducible evaluation. Gate I can focus on one earlier graduate topic, but must include baselines, ablations, uncertainty and limitations. Publication acceptance is not required; credible independent evaluation is. Preserve unsuccessful experiments and distinguish a reproduced known result from the learner's actual extension.
lessons.example: A new vector instruction that saves arithmetic but increases packing and spills may lose in the full engine. The experiment must measure both the generated kernel and its application integration.
lessons.lab: Complete Gate I and defend one compiler transformation's legality. Pass: an independent reader reruns the central experiment, the claimed extension is precisely identified and raw evidence supports the conclusions.
lessons.reading: R14 and R48: compilation and architecture; R49: co-design methodology; Module 41: research evaluation protocol.

quiz.question: Why can a faster instruction fail to improve the application?
quiz.answer: Packing, spills, data movement or unaccelerated work can outweigh the arithmetic savings.

quiz.question: What distinguishes reproduction from extension?
quiz.answer: Reproduction recreates an existing result; extension changes or adds a clearly identified method, setting or analysis.

quiz.question: Is publication acceptance mandatory for Gate I?
quiz.answer: No. The requirement is rigorous, reproducible work and an independent technical review.

sections: Explain the mechanism across the software/hardware boundary

A compiler transformation can change instruction count, data layout, register pressure, cache behavior and parallel occupancy at once. Attribute a claimed gain to evidence, not to the name of an instruction or architecture. A wider vector operation may require packing, unpacking, alignment handling and scalar tails. Saving arithmetic can increase memory traffic or reduce the number of resident workers.

Build a cost decomposition that links the generated code to the application's critical path. Compare a competent software baseline before proposing an accelerator or new instruction. An ablation should remove the proposed mechanism while keeping unrelated improvements fixed. A sensitivity study should vary a parameter that can expose the mechanism's limits, such as batch size, arithmetic intensity or register demand.
Complete one coherent research argument

Gate I requires a bounded reproduction plus a clearly identified extension, new setting or rigorous failure analysis. State exactly what prior result you are testing, which assumptions you retained and how your comparison differs. A reproduction discrepancy can become useful evidence when investigated carefully; it is not permission to invent a matching result or silently retune the baseline.

Deliver the derivation or semantic proof, code, workload definitions, raw data, analysis scripts, one ablation, one sensitivity study and a limitations section. Use equal-quality comparisons when methods change quality with speed. Identify the trial unit behind uncertainty estimates. Preserve negative cases and the tuning/evaluation split. This work prepares the thesis; it does not need to establish global novelty or publication acceptance.
The reviewer must be able to challenge the central claim

An independent reader should build or run the artifact and regenerate its main table from raw data. Ask the reader to inspect one failed case, alter one input and explain the legality or numerical assumptions behind the main transformation. Record discrepancies and revisions. A README that says results are reproducible is not evidence that another person actually reproduced them. [S14]

Even when Gate I focuses on rendering or simulation, this module still requires the small compiler optimization with semantic tests and generated-code inspection. The volume's breadth exercises support the specialization rather than disappearing once a favorite topic is chosen. Completion is recorded as demonstrated self-study work, with pending GPU, hardware or independent-review evidence marked honestly.
expansion.worked: An engine frame takes 12 ms: 3 ms in a candidate kernel and 9 ms elsewhere. A proposed instruction halves the kernel arithmetic, apparently saving 1.5 ms. But the new layout adds 0.8 ms of packing and 0.9 ms of extra spill/transfer work. The new frame takes 9+1.5+0.8+0.9=12.2 ms, so speedup is 12/12.2, approximately 0.984. The kernel-only 2x number is real under its narrow boundary, but the integrated change is a regression. A sound report can conclude that the instruction is unattractive for this workload without treating the experiment as a failure of learning.
procedure: Choose one Gate I depth track and freeze the central claim, baseline and evaluation protocol.
Finish the required compiler mini-project even when the research track is elsewhere.
Run held-out, adverse, ablation and parameter-sensitivity cases with raw evidence preserved.
Regenerate the main table from scripts and connect each row to source, configuration and input identity.
Have an independent reviewer reproduce the central result, inspect a failed case and question the derivation or legality argument.
Revise the claim to match the evidence and prepare a handoff identifying open questions for Volume 10.
checks: Reproduction and extension are separately named.
The baseline is competent and comparisons honor the quality contract.
Ablation, sensitivity and failure evidence exist.
Independent review is documented, not simulated by a self-check.
The compiler requirement and any pending device validation remain visible.
problems: P1. Compute the application speedup in the worked example and explain why the 2x kernel number is insufficient.
P2. A reviewer can run the code but cannot regenerate the main table because scene files are missing. Has Gate I passed?
solutions: P1. 12/12.2 is about 0.984, a slowdown of roughly 1.7% in elapsed time. Packing and spill/transfer overhead outweigh the arithmetic savings. The timing boundary determines what the 2x number supports.

P2. No. Executable code alone is insufficient for the central reproducibility requirement. Supply authorized inputs or an adequately scoped replacement experiment, rerun it and narrow the claim as necessary.
